The Community has brought back one of our most cherished analogue traditions: the Lomographers’ Print Exchange. Since then, we have constantly been reminded of the simple yet magical act of sending and receiving photographs to connect one film lover to another.

Over the past months, prints have crossed borders across the globe – from Brazil to Australia, Hong Kong to Spain, Poland to the United States, and more. We caught up with a few participants to see how their exchanges went down, inviting them to look back on the prints they sent and the postcards that have since found their way into their mailboxes.

@agafa from Latvia: Personalized Prints For Each Recipient

What I Sent

After I received replies from other Lomographers, I started choosing which photos to print. I decided to make each postcard unique, so every participant received a different image that I felt matched their style and interests. I chose some of my favorite shots, including vibrant street scenes and colorful everyday moments. In total, I sent around 15 to 20 postcards to Lomographers in Japan, the USA, Australia, Spain, Finland, Romania, Belarus, France, Chile, and Brazil.

The whole process was incredibly exciting. Before selecting a print, I carefully explored each person's LomoHome to find a photo that I thought they would truly enjoy. It made the exchange feel much more personal, and I loved the idea that every postcard was chosen especially for its recipient.

Credits: agafa

What I Received

The first postcard I received was from Japan. I was absolutely thrilled! From that moment on, I checked my mailbox every single day because I couldn't wait to see what would arrive next. It felt like opening a surprise gift or an Advent calendar before Christmas. Seeing these prints in person is a completely different experience from viewing photos online. You can appreciate the paper, the colors, and the personal touch that each sender put into their postcard. To keep them safe, I bought a photo album where I now carefully store my growing collection.

Credits: agafa

@laracakmak from Spain: Sharing a Piece of Barcelona

What I Sent

I chose to send a photo of Somorrostro Beach in Barcelona, featuring El Peix, Frank Gehry’s iconic fish sculpture. I love the way the sunlight reflects off its metal scales, making it sparkle throughout the day. The sculpture was created for the 1992 Olympic Games, a time that completely transformed this part of the city. I was a child then, and I still remember visiting the area with my school to watch the construction progress. What had once been an industrial port became a vibrant waterfront welcoming athletes from around the world. Back then, Barcelona’s slogan was “Barcelona, posa’t guapa” (“Barcelona, make yourself beautiful”), and that spirit of renewal has always stayed with me. I wanted to share a place that represents both my city and my childhood memories.

Credits: laracakmak

What I Received

Receiving postcards from Lomographers around the world has been one of my favorite experiences this year. As a child, my friends and I always exchanged postcards when we traveled, and I’ve missed that tradition ever since. Every postcard I received felt personal, showcasing a unique technique and a place or subject that meant something to its creator. Some even shared memories of visiting my city. A few postcards were lost on both sides along the way, but that’s part of the adventure.

Thanks to my dear Lomographers: @agostc, @amy\bellezza, @anttihoo, @atzipinki, @barker\days\ahead, @carnivalnoon, @crismiranda, @cul-de-sac, @eara, @elianarchivist, @elsvanopstal, @evelynedierikx, @frenchyfyl, and @akio\nakai.

I’m especially grateful to @evelynedierikx for the photo booklet, prints, and postcards. I love the theme of angels, so her work was particularly meaningful to me. I keep all of them together in my journal, as a collection of memories and inspiration.

Credits: laracakmak

@fabio\_corsatto from Italy: Snaps of Landscapes and Feline Friends

What I Sent

I usually photograph portraits, but for this exchange, I chose to send landscapes captured during short trips and a few pictures of my cats – these are photos that I normally don’t post on any social media platform except the Lomography website. There wasn’t any particular reason behind this choice. They were simply images I liked and felt like sharing.

So far, I’ve exchanged postcards with Akio ( @akio\nakai) from Japan, João ( @shoao) from Brazil, JL ( @smwh\in) from Germany, Gunnison ( @gunnisonlee) from the United States, Philippe ( @frenchyfyl) from France, Igor ( @klubttu) from the United Kingdom, and Laura ( @eara) from Austria.

I still keep sending postcards to this day. Sometimes they get lost along the way or are returned to me even though the address is correct, but that doesn’t discourage me. I just resend them. After all, this too is part of the beauty of a photographic exchange through the mail.

Credits: @fabio\_corsatto

What I Received

Working in a photography shop and taking care of other people’s photographs is part of my daily routine. Receiving these postcards, however, was something completely different.

What I enjoyed the most was waiting – not knowing what would arrive, who had chosen that particular photograph, or when it would be delivered to me. Each postcard was a little surprise, and I always felt joy and warmth knowing that somewhere in the world, someone had thought of me and decided to send me that photograph. Each postcard traveled from one country to another before reaching my hands, and that makes them even more special.

I keep all the postcards in a box at the shop where I work, and from time to time, I like to show them to anyone who comes in. I want to thank the people that allowed me to participate in this project and those that exchanged this experience with me!

Credits: @fabio\_corsatto

@shoao from Brazil: Special Envelopes of Photos and Stories

What I Sent

I selected 40 photos and printed them on silk-finish photographic paper. Everyone I exchanged prints with received a unique print. I also tried to include something meaningful with each one – a behind-the-scenes story or a bit of context about where and how the photograph was made. Inside each envelope, I added a few smaller prints from my early analogue years and, in some cases, a piece from an old project of mine called Postcards from the End of the World.

I sent prints to Italy, Germany, the Czech Republic, Canada, the United States, Greece, France, Brazil, the United Kingdom, Austria, Finland, New Zealand, Argentina, Spain, Chile, Romania, and Georgia. Isn't it beautiful how far an idea can travel?

Credits: @wil6ka, @ketchfoto, & @mackiechartres (sent by @shoao)

What I Received

The first postcard I received was from @fabio\_corsatto. There’s something special about receiving a letter with a printed photo and a handwritten message from another country. That's something we should never lose.

After the first one, more kept arriving, and the feeling was always the same. This community is amazing. Keep sending postcards. Letters. Anything. We could all use a little more of that.

Credits: @shoao

@agostc from Argentina: Sending Travel Souvenirs to the World

What I Sent

I sent some photos I took during trips to different places, mostly of rooms or landscapes that gave me a sense of being somewhere else in the world. I felt like sharing that feeling of being in another part of the globe because it's similar to sending a postcard: a small part of you travels to an unexpected place. That's how I ended up sending photos to people living in Ireland, Italy, the United States, the Philippines, Georgia, Estonia, Belarus, Spain, and Argentina.

Credits: agostc

What I Received

Every time I knew someone had sent me a postcard, I checked my mailbox every day until it arrived. I get that same feeling whenever I take a roll of film to the photo lab. That's why shooting on film, printing photos, and sending postcards feel so special to me. It's completely different from the fast-paced, instant nature of the digital world. I also love the way you connect with other Lomography members by expressing your gratitude for each exchange. That's why I keep all the postcards in a special box, together with other meaningful postcards I've received from my family or for my birthday.

Credits: agostc

Birmingham Design Festival was created by designers Daniel Alcorn and Luke Tonge and is an annual celebration of local, national and international designers who come together for a packed program of talks, workshops and events from some of the most innovative people in the industry. This year, we brought a bit of Lomography magic to Birmingham with a special LomoApparat LomoWalk around the graffiti-clad streets of Digbeth using some LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100-400 and LomoChrome Turquoise 35 mm film, and a whole lot of Kaleidoscope, multiple exposure, and Splitzer experimentation.

Photos by Hannah Brown \| Taken on the Lomo MC-A

In true Birmingham-style, the day started out rainy and grey, and switched to glorious sunshine as soon as we stepped outside. We set up this walk in Digbeth, Birmingham's very own creative quarter. It's an old industrial area that has been appropriated by artists and creatives who make the most of the Victorian factory building to set up art studios and offices.

Photos by Lauren Skillman \| Shot with the LomoApparat & LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100-400

There are some impressive graffiti murals dotted around in the most unexpected corners of Digbeth and, as you can see form the photos results, our participants really set to work photographing as much as they could.

We talked to one of the participants, Lauren Skillman, about her experience of this LomoWalk.

Craig Smith, Michela Dunn and friends of John Hall \| Shot with the LomoApparat & LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100-400

Hello Lauren, please tell us why you signed up to this walk.

I’ve been on lots of group photo walks and photomarathons before, trying various kinds of cameras wherever possible. Lomography was new to me, and I was keen to experiment with the interesting color filters and gritty textures it can create.

It was nice to do a practical workshop in addition to seeing the talks at Birmingham Design Festival, and events like this are a great chance to meet people with similar creative interests.

Splitzer and Kaleidoscope madness by XX \| Shot with the LomoApparat and the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400

How did you find the experience and shooting with the LomoApparat?

The LomoApparat was similar to a \[point-and-shoot\] camera but with extra features, and we were also given lenses to experiment with. It took a moment to get used to not being able to see the effects through the viewfinder. After some practice, I gained intuition in what was worth taking a photo of (there were only 36 opportunities on the film reel), and which subjects would work well together when layered on top of each other via double exposure.

Charlotte Powell, John Hall and Margot Edwards \| Shot with the LomoApparat and the LomoChrome Turquoise 35 mm film

How did you find the results, and do you think you would try shooting film again?

Around 1/3 of the images came out as hoped. The kaleidoscope lens created fun fragmented shots and was most effective when there was a solid and vibrant subject like the street art/graffiti around Digbeth. The camera was a bit limited without a zoom or focus, so some images came out blurry. And of course, I got the classic accidental finger in shot! I didn’t put any pressure on myself to get ‘perfect’ shots though because it was my first time doing Lomography, but I would definitely work with film again to develop my experience with the craft. That said, my visual style is quite abstract and surreal, so I liked being pleasantly surprised by the quirky outcomes!

A huge thank you to everyone who took part and made this event such a success! To find out more about Birmingham Design Festival visit their website.

Nuevos niños es James Beghelli's el último proyecto fotográfico, llevado del deseo de dejar que la adolescencia cuente su propia historia. Es inmediata, sin reclutar, y no necesita ninguna explicación; un intento de entrar en la vida diaria de las generaciones más jóvenes, retrocediendo como observador externo y dándoles una cámara, confiando en que ellos capturen su propia realidad.

© James Beghelli con el Simple Use Camera y Lady Grey B&W 35 mm ISO 400

El proyecto tenía como objetivo explorar la vida cotidiana de los adolescentes, capturando su autenticidad y espontaneidad. La idea era alejarse de los estereotipos y preconcepciones asociados con esta etapa de la vida inmersándonos en el mundo de los adolescentes y dejarles contar sus propias historias a través de imágenes.

Para lograr esto, James usó nuestro Simple Use Cameras cargado con el LomoChrome Color ’92 Sun-kissed 35 mm ISO 400 y el Lady Grey B&W 35 mm ISO 400. Estas herramientas esenciales e intuitivas fueron elegidas específicamente para permitir que los adolescentes los usaran para seguir sus instintos.

© James Beghelli con el Simple Use Camera y Lady Grey B&W 35 mm ISO 400

El proceso analógico impone un ritmo más lento, con un período de espera que contrasta con la inmediatez de la fotografía digital. También invita a una interacción más reflexiva con el acto de la fotografía. La ausencia de un avance mejora la espontaneidad e imprevisibilidad del resultado, que refleja perfectamente la esencia de la adolescencia.

El proyecto fue diseñado para superar los estereotipos asociados a menudo con la adolescencia y presentar una perspectiva más directa, instintiva e infiltrada sobre el tema.

© James Beghelli con el Simple Use Camera y LomoChrome Color ’92 Sun-kissed 35 mm ISO 400

Para establecer un terreno común con los participantes, James aprovechó su experiencia personal e identificó tres áreas que dieron forma a su desarrollo. La primera área es un sentido de pertenencia vinculada al graffiti y a los espacios urbanos como lugares de reunión e identidad. La segunda zona es interacción social, que ocurre en espacios de ensayo, en conciertos, fiestas y otros entornos sociales. La tercera área es exploración, que experimentó a través de un movimiento constante alrededor de la ciudad, viajando por bicicleta o scooter y sus contactos.

© James Beghelli con el Simple Use Camera y LomoChrome Color ’92 Sun-kissed 35 mm ISO 400

En lugar de imponer una estructura rígida, estas categorías se utilizaron como puntos de contacto para fomentar una relación con los jóvenes involucrados. Cada participante creó su propia narrativa visual, utilizando la cámara como una herramienta personal y directa.

© James Beghelli con el Simple Use Camera y LomoChrome Color ’92 Sun-kissed 35 mm ISO 400

El resultado de la primera fase fue deliberadamente dejado abierto. Las imágenes producidas no se adhieren a un estilo particular o estética impuesta desde el exterior.

En cambio, surgieron fragmentos de vida real, capturando momentos cotidianos, gestos espontáneos y situaciones íntimas o compartidas. Esta falta de control se convirtió en el corazón del proyecto porque refleja la misma naturaleza de la adolescencia: inestable, cambiante y no completamente descifrable.

© James Beghelli con el Simple Use Camera y LomoChrome Color ’92 Sun-kissed 35 mm ISO 400

En la segunda fase, James Beghelli trabajó con el material recogido. Las fotografías de los estudiantes formaron la base de una nueva composición visual, enriquecida por retratos y todavía vive. El objetivo no era corregir o reinterpretar, sino dar forma y continuidad a lo que ya había surgido, y crear un diálogo entre perspectivas internas y externas.

© James Beghelli con el Simple Use Camera y Lady Grey B&W 35 mm ISO 400

En general, Nuevos niños se presenta como un pequeño manifiesto visual que busca restaurar la complejidad a una generación que a menudo se superpone o se reduce a clichés. A través de este proyecto, James Beghelli examinó los códigos de una generación y, al mismo tiempo, se refleja en su propia adolescencia, tratando de llamar la atención a este crucial pero fugaz período de formación de identidad.

Gracias, James, por compartir su proyecto de fotografía analógica con nosotros! Para ver más de su trabajo, no te olvides de seguirlo Instagram.

New Kids is James Beghelli's latest photography project, borne out of the desire to let adolescence tell its own story. It is unmediated, unscripted, and needs no explanation; an attempt to enter the daily lives of younger generations by stepping back as an outside observer and giving them a camera, trusting them to capture their own reality.

© James Beghelli with the Simple Use Camera and Lady Grey B&W 35 mm ISO 400

The project aimed to explore the daily lives of teenagers, capturing their authenticity and spontaneity. The idea was to move away from the stereotypes and preconceptions associated with this life stage by immersing ourselves in the teenagers' world and letting them tell their own stories through images.

To achieve this, James used our Simple Use Cameras loaded with the LomoChrome Color ’92 Sun-kissed 35 mm ISO 400 and the Lady Grey B&W 35 mm ISO 400. These essential, intuitive tools were chosen specifically to allow the teenagers using them to follow their instincts.

© James Beghelli with the Simple Use Camera and Lady Grey B&W 35 mm ISO 400

Film as a medium is no coincidental choice. The analogue process imposes a slower pace, with a waiting period that contrasts with the immediacy of digital photography. It also invites a more reflective interaction with the act of photography. The absence of a preview enhances the spontaneity and unpredictability of the result, which perfectly reflects the essence of adolescence.

The project was designed to overcome the stereotypes often associated with adolescence and present a more direct, instinctive, and unfiltered perspective on the topic.

© James Beghelli with the Simple Use Camera and LomoChrome Color ’92 Sun-kissed 35 mm ISO 400

To establish common ground with the participants, James drew on his personal experience and identified three areas that shaped his development. The first area is a sense of belonging linked to graffiti and urban spaces as places of gathering and identity. The second area is social interaction, which occurs in rehearsal spaces, at concerts, parties, and other social settings. The third area is exploration, which he experienced through constant movement around the city, traveling by bike or scooter, and ongoing connections with his group of friends.

© James Beghelli with the Simple Use Camera and LomoChrome Color ’92 Sun-kissed 35 mm ISO 400

Rather than imposing a rigid structure, these categories were used as points of contact to foster a relationship with the young people involved. Each participant created their own visual narrative, using the camera as a personal and direct tool.

© James Beghelli with the Simple Use Camera and LomoChrome Color ’92 Sun-kissed 35 mm ISO 400

The outcome of the first phase was deliberately left open-ended. The images produced did not adhere to a particular style or aesthetic imposed from the outside.

Instead, fragments of real life emerged, capturing everyday moments, spontaneous gestures, and intimate or shared situations. This lack of control became the heart of the project because it reflects the very nature of adolescence: unstable, changeable, and not entirely decipherable.

© James Beghelli with the Simple Use Camera and LomoChrome Color ’92 Sun-kissed 35 mm ISO 400

In the second phase, James Beghelli worked with the collected material. The students' photographs formed the basis of a new visual composition, enriched by portraits and still lives. The focus was not on correcting or reinterpreting, but on giving form and continuity to what had already emerged, and creating a dialogue between internal and external perspectives.

© James Beghelli with the Simple Use Camera and Lady Grey B&W 35 mm ISO 400

Overall, New Kids presents itself as a small visual manifesto that seeks to restore complexity to a generation that is often oversimplified or reduced to clichés. Through this project, James Beghelli examined the codes of a generation and, at the same time, reflected on his own adolescence, attempting to draw attention to this crucial yet fleeting period of identity formation.

Thank you, James, for sharing your analogue photography project with us! To see more of his work, don't forget to follow him on Instagram.

Algunos fines de semana están empacados desde el momento en que despiertes hasta que termines por la noche. Con tantas cosas pasando, deberías tener una cosa menos que pensar - entrar en el Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera! Su formato compacto y en marcha asegura que usted está listo para enfrentar ese itinerario relleno.

Lea como escritores de la revista Lomography @francinegaebriele y @nate\_soriano prueba el rendimiento de la cámara durante todo un día – en la amplia luz del día en parques y cafés hasta después de que el sol se pone durante conciertos y paseos nocturnos.

Créditos: @francinegaebriele & @nate\_soriano \ torturado con la Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera utilizando Lomography Color Negative 35 mm 800

Hora del día con @francinegaebriele: Disparo donde el Sol brilla

Anteriormente he visto lo bien que la cámara se hacía con flash en un día de sobrecast, así que quería despojar las cosas y ver cómo funcionaba completamente por sí sola. Para esta sesión, dependí exclusivamente de la luz solar – ningún flash o cualquier otra técnica agregada, para abrazar el atractivo directo de la cámara de película de uso simple de medio marco recargable!

Para la primera mitad de esta prueba de día y noche, estaba ansioso por dejar que la luz natural hiciera toda la magia.

Créditos: @francinegaebriele \ torturado con la Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera utilizando Lomochrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200 (primera foto) " Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800 (segundo a cuarto fotos)

Había estado lloviendo en mi área durante semanas, pero esperé pacientemente para el día perfecto de sol antes de sacar la cámara para dar una vuelta. Tan pronto como los cielos se despejaron, hice lo que normalmente haría cuando tengo una cámara de medio marco en la mano: vagaba donde el día me llevó y fotografiaba todo lo que cogía mi ojo. Con tantos marcos para rellenar, me sentí emocionado de presionar el obturador mientras iba por mi día sin preocuparse por mi pelaje.

Bajo la luz solar directa, la cámara produjo algunos de los marcos más nítidos del rollo. Junto con la distancia de tiro derecha (0.6m a 1,5m), los detalles de mis tomas salieron sorprendentemente afilados. Cuando estás filmando durante un día soleado, todo lo que realmente tienes que hacer es prestar atención al rango de enfoque de la cámara para lograr sin esfuerzo resultados limpios.

Créditos: @francinegaebriele \ torturado con la Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera utilizando Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

Otra cosa que noté fue cuánto la calidad de la luz cambió significativamente cada fotografía. Incluso en una tarde brillante, entrar en la sombra podría cambiar notablemente la mirada de su disparo. Áreas tocadas por el detalle de la luz solar directa retenida hermosamente, mientras que porciones ligeramente más oscuras se volverían más grana y tienen sombras más profundas.

Un buen ejemplo de esto es uno de mis marcos favoritos del rollo: una estantería iluminada por una ventana cercana. La luz del sol aterrizó perfectamente en una sola fila de libros de colores brillantes y la cámara capturó ese contraste muy bien. Me encanta cómo preservaba la calidez de la luz exterior mientras dejaba que los estantes circundantes se escondieran en las sombras.

Créditos: @francinegaebriele \ torturado con la Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera utilizando Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

Incluso en tono más pesado, creo que la cámara todavía se hizo la luz bellamente. Las imágenes pueden no tener el mismo nivel de detalle que los tomados bajo la luz solar directa o con flash, pero tenían un ambiente cálido y acogedor que todavía me gusta personalmente.

Un café que visité por la mañana fue protegido del sol entre edificios altos. A pesar de eso, su exterior de madera tomó un aspecto suave y hogareño que se tradujo hermosamente en la película. Estos disparos podrían haber perdido algunos detalles debido a los colores mudos y el grano, pero creo que realmente capturó la mañana lenta que tenía en ese momento!

Créditos: @francinegaebriele \ torturado con la Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera utilizando Lomochrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

Para el tiro al día, una buena regla del pulgar es utilizar el flash cuando estás en zonas sombreadas – incluyendo interiores incluso cuando hay luz natural que viene a través de ventanas. También ayuda a familiarizarse con how different ISO speeds perform in various lighting conditionsEn mi caso, empecé con el precargado Lomochrome Classicolor 200 y reloaded la cámara con Lomography Color Negative 800. Tomando nota mental de la ISO de mi película hizo mucho más fácil decidir cómo me acerqué a las escenas y me dio una mejor idea de cómo serían los resultados.

Entonces, de nuevo, si prefieres los disparos más de humor, no tengas miedo de abrazar cualquier luz disponible que hay, y confía en la cámara de película de uso simple de medio marco para hacer su trabajo!

Noche con @nate\_soriano: Framing the After-Hour Frenzy

Las cámaras más desechables tienen un cuchillo para luchar en condiciones de poca luz debido a la falta de ajustes ajustables, pero veamos cómo la cámara de película recargable de uso simple de medio marco precargada con LomoChrome Classicolor ISO 200 se apila contra la multitud. Para esta prueba, decidí disparar estrictamente con flash on (st I waste a perfectamente good roll on 72 pictures of the gigmus out).

La primera ubicación fue un restaurante de la década de los 50 situado en la Poblacion de la ciudad de Makati. Al principio, las fotos presentaron grano prominente. Esto es probablemente un resultado de disparos en 200 ISO interiores por la noche, aunque apoyado por fuentes de luz externas (es decir, luces de techo, lámparas, etc.). A pesar de esto, los colores permanecieron vibrantes como se ve en los pops de granos rojos y azules en el restaurante excéntrico

La cámara luchó un poco en ciertas partes, como cómo disparar lejos del tema, especialmente en la configuración exterior, conduce a la subexposición como se ve en la foto de los signos de neón abajo. Nuestra punta sería acercarse para compensar la gama flash de la cámara, asegurando que su sujeto está bien iluminado.

Créditos: @nate\_soriano \ torturado con la Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera utilizando Lomochrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

El próximo lugar fue un espacio interior incluso dimmer, iluminado sólo por algunos focos rojos en las esquinas del escenario. La cámara de medio marco se mantuvo sorprendentemente bien teniendo en cuenta que estaba cargada con la película ISO 200.

Me di cuenta de que con esta fotografo, los colores aparecieron más planas cuanto más lejos estaba la cámara del tema, lo que me llevó a concluir que un buen calibre al disparar con flash en ISO 200 estaría alrededor de la longitud de un brazo para asegurar la exposición suficiente para un contraste más agudo (esto se muestra en la foto del artista con pelo azul abajo).

Créditos: @nate\_soriano \ torturado con la Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera utilizando Lomochrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

Para el último área de probar la cámara en la película ISO 200, fui al parque local de diversiones. En las tres primeras fotos, no había mucho de un problema dado que las cabinas del juego estaban lo suficientemente iluminadas para añadir otra fuente de luz.

Créditos: @nate\_soriano \ torturado con la Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera utilizando Lomochrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

Al ver como la cámara luchó un poco con ISO 200, decidí cargar en un rollo más rápido. Aquí es donde la cámara brillaba más por la noche. Recargar la cámara de uso simple de medio marco con la Lomography Color Negative ISO 800 era, en palabras de beabadoobee, el par perfecto Como se ve a continuación, las imágenes tenían un grano más fino a pesar de ser tomadas con la película ISO 800. Los colores también presentaron un mejor contraste, los negros eran más oscuros, y más detalles fueron capturados dentro de cada escena.

Créditos: @nate\_soriano \ torturado con la Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera utilizando Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

El último lugar en el que probé la cámara en la película ISO 800 fue en un bar durante un Car Seat Headrest Noche En comparación con las fotos anteriores del concierto tomadas con ISO 200, las fotos de esta vez estaban bien saturadas a pesar de lo tenue que era el lugar. En una nota personal, creo que sus no frills, la naturaleza de punta y punta lo solidifica como un sidekick de fotografía en marcha.

Créditos: @nate\_soriano \ torturado con la Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera utilizando Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

Some weekends are just packed from the moment you wake up until you wind down at night. With so much going on, you ought to have one less thing to think about - enter the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera! Its compact, on-the-go format ensures that you’re ready to face that stuffed itinerary.

Read along as Lomography Magazine writers @francinegaebriele and @nate\_soriano test the camera’s performance throughout an entire day – in the broad daylight at parks and cafes until after the sun sets during gigs and evening walks.

Credits: @francinegaebriele & @nate\_soriano \| Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera using Lomography Color Negative 35 mm 800

Daytime with @francinegaebriele: Shooting Where the Sun Shines

I’ve previously seen how well the camera performed with flash on an overcast day, so I wanted to strip things back and see how it worked completely on its own. For this shoot, I relied solely on sunlight – no flash or any other added techniques, to embrace the straightforward appeal of the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera!

For the first half of this day-and-night test, I was eager to let natural light do all the magic.

Credits: @francinegaebriele \| Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera using Lomochrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200 (first photo) & Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800 (second to fourth photos)

It had been raining in my area for weeks, but I waited patiently for the perfect sunny day before taking the camera out for a spin. As soon as the skies cleared, I did as I normally would when I have a half-frame camera in hand: wandered wherever the day took me and photographed whatever caught my eye. With so many frames to fill, I felt excited to press the shutter as I went about my day not worrying about using my roll frugally.

Under direct sunlight, the camera produced some of the crispiest frames from the roll. Paired with the right shooting distance (0.6m to 1.5m), the details of my shots came out surprisingly sharp. When you’re shooting during a sunny day, all you really have to do is pay attention to the camera’s focusing range in order to effortlessly achieve clean results.

Credits: @francinegaebriele \| Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera using Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

Another thing I noticed was how much the quality of light significantly changed each photograph. Even on a bright afternoon, stepping into the shade could noticeably change the look of your shot. Areas touched by direct sunlight retained detail beautifully, while slightly darker portions would become grainier and have deeper shadows.

A good example of this is one of my favorite frames from the roll: a bookshelf illuminated by a nearby window. The sunlight landed perfectly on a single row of brightly colored books and the camera captured that contrast really well. I love how it preserved the warmth of the light outside while letting the surrounding shelves just hide in the shadows.

Credits: @francinegaebriele \| Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera using Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

Even in heavier shade, I think the camera still rendered light beautifully. The images may not have the same level of detail as those taken under direct sunlight or with flash, but they had a warm, cozy atmosphere that I still personally like.

One café that I visited in the morning was sheltered from the sun in between tall buildings. Despite that, its wooden exterior took on a soft, homey look that translated beautifully on film. These shots might have lost some details due to the muted colors and grain, but I think it really captured the slow morning that I had at the time!

Credits: @francinegaebriele \| Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera using Lomochrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

For daytime shooting, a good rule of thumb is to use the flash when you’re in shaded areas – including indoors even when there’s natural light coming through windows. It also helps to familiarize yourself with how different ISO speeds perform in various lighting conditions. In my case, I started with the preloaded Lomochrome Classicolor 200 and reloaded the camera with Lomography Color Negative 800. Taking a mental note of my film’s ISO made it much easier to decide how I approached the scenes and gave me a better idea of what the results would look like.

Then again, if you prefer moodier shots, don’t be afraid to embrace whatever available light there is, and trust the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera to do its job!

Nighttime with @nate\_soriano: Framing the After-Hour Frenzy

Most disposable cameras have a knack for struggling in low-light conditions because of the lack of adjustable settings, but let's see how the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera pre-loaded with LomoChrome Classicolor ISO 200 stacks up against the crowd. I also took the camera out to three different places that I felt was teeming with nightlife energy: (1) A restaurant; (2) A gig at a bar; and (3) An amusement park.

The first location was a 1950s diner-esque restaurant situated in Makati City's Poblacion. On the onset, the photos featured prominent grain. This is most likely a result of shooting at 200 ISO indoors at night, albeit supported by external light sources (i.e. ceiling lights, lamps, etc.). Despite this, colors remained vibrant as seen in the pops of reds and blues in the eccentric decor of the restaurant, and the grain added an extra layer of texture that blended well with the vintage theme.

The camera did struggle a little in certain parts, such as how shooting far from the subject, especially in outdoor settings, leads to underexposure as seen in the photo of neon signs below. Our tip would be to get closer to compensate for the flash range of the camera, assuring that your subject is well lit.

Credits: @nate\_soriano \| Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera using Lomochrome Classicolor 35 mm ISO 200

The next venue was an even dimmer indoor space, lit only by a few red spotlights in the corners of the stage. The half-frame camera held up surprisingly well considering that it was loaded with ISO 200 film.

I noticed that with this photoset, colors appeared flatter the further the camera was away from the subject, leading me to conclude that a good gauge when shooting with flash at ISO 200 would be around an arm's length to ensure just enough exposure for sharper contrast (this is showcased in the photo of the artist with blue hair below).

I was thoroughly impressed with how quick the camera captured photos, keeping up with the energy of the crowd. ¿Dónde fue el último lugar que se tomó una radiografía? En el siglo XXI la respuesta parece obvia: en el hospital después de unos pocos huesos rotos. Rebobinar cien años, sin embargo, y usted podría encontrar la radiografía, o la fotografía de rayos X, en algunos lugares bastante extraños. La invención de la radiografía en 1895 rápidamente se puso bajo la piel del público en general, y se convirtió en una forma de arte fotográfico y entretenimiento en sus primeros días tanto como un jugador médico.

La explosión instantánea de las radiografías en el mundo cotidiano fue de alto riesgo, una gran recompensa ya que los peligros que venían con esta nueva tecnología inicialmente no se dieron cuenta y se entendieron mal. Nunca antes las imágenes de interiores inspiraron la fotografía experimental y el arte, pero también las cuestiones existenciales sobre la vida y la muerte.

Murex inflatus (Riesenstachelschnecke), Röntgenaufnahme, Frtiz Block, 1931. X-ray image of real pearls (middle) and fake pearls (left and right), tomado por Walter König en Physikalischer Verein, 1896. X-ray of a flower, extracted from The story of X-rays from Röntgen to Isotopes.png), 1960, Wikimedia Commons.

Durante un corto período de su historia, la fotografía de rayos X estaba en manos públicas antes de que cambiaran las normas de seguridad y la conciencia, dejándonos con algunas imágenes únicas que no son capaces de recrearse a la misma escala en el mundo moderno de la fotografía.

Invención y existencialismo

¡He visto mi muerte!

Esta fue la reacción a la primera radiografía humana del mundo. Anna Bertha Röntgen, mirando una imagen de sus propios dedos esqueléticos y anillo de boda (ver abajo), fue inicialmente horrorizada por el descubrimiento de su esposo. La Dra. Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, después de semanas de experimentación, acababa de aprovechar accidentalmente el poder de desconocido, o “X”, raya y probó a su esposa.

Hand mit Ringen (Hand with Rings)Wilhelm Röntgen, 1896, Wikimedia Commons. A compass whose magnetic needle is entirely surrounded by metal, viewed through x-ray, W.K. von Röntgen, 1895, Wikimedia Commons. One block of glass, one of aluminium, two of calcite and two of quartz, viewed under x-rayWilhelm Conrad Röntgen, 1895, Wikimedia Commons.

Transitionando desde una pantalla fluorescente a placas de vidrio fotosensibles, captó con éxito los misteriosos rayos en una imagen fija y comenzó a investigar sus propiedades. Además de fotografiar la mano de su esposa, experimentó con metales y objetos cotidianos. Estas fotografías iniciales se utilizaron para compartir su nuevo conocimiento públicamente.

The door of Röntgen's laboratory, with a platinum plate attached to the handle, viewed under x-rayFotografia de la radiografía de W.K. von Röntgen, 1895. de Wilhelm Konrad von Röntgen - 1895 - Wellcome Collection, Reino Unido - CC BY.

El poder de las radiografías, o los rayos Röntgen, como a veces se les llama todavía, era innegable, y el Dr. Röntgen pronto hizo su descubrimiento visible a la sociedad sin patente debido a su valor científico. Su uso médico fue por supuesto un punto de interés inmediato, pero las fotografías de rayos X a mediados de los años 90 tuvieron un largo camino por recorrer antes de convertirse en la práctica médica especializada y exclusiva que son hoy.

¿Cuánto tiene que ver esto con la fotografía?

Arte de rayos X temprano: Flores, Fotografía & Ferias divertidas

Las noticias de las radiografías viajaron muy rápidamente, y los radiografos se estaban recreando dentro de los meses del primer anuncio de Röntgen sobre las habilidades de los rayos misteriosos. Después de la emoción pública generalizada sobre el fenómeno, pronto llegaron manifestaciones públicas de rayos X y experiencias interactivas.

Aún sin darse cuenta de los riesgos de la radiación, se hizo posible tener fotografías de rayos X hechas de manos, cabezas, o bolsas durante ferias y carnavales para llevar a casa como recuerdo. Así es, no se necesitan huesos rotos – simplemente entretenimiento de exposición interminable para toda la familia! Incluso era posible comprar equipo DIY para hacer sus propias imágenes de radiografía en casa.

Glasgow's X-ray campaign against tuberculosis, 11 de marzo a 12 de abril de 1957, The Wellcome Collection. X-ray postcard advertisement.jpg), la colección Werner Von Boltenstern de LMU, Wikimedia Commons.

Las radiografías aparecieron en muchos lugares inusuales a principios del siglo XX, incluyendo publicidad, tiendas de zapatos y cine durante lo que se consideraba un período de rayos X Mania. Del mismo modo a la tendencia anterior de spirit photography, algunas personas esperaban que la radiografía pudiera demostrar la existencia de entidades invisibles, como los espíritus o el alma.

No toda la opinión pública era positiva – había mucha preocupación y sátira sobre el potencial uso indebido de imágenes de rayos X, como mirar indecentemente en cuerpos vecinos bajo su ropa o entrometiendo en el contenido de la bolsa de alguien. Algunas personas incluso creían que íbamos a empezar a leer en los pensamientos de los demás gracias a estos misteriosos y maliciosos rayos.

Un poema satírico publicado en Fotografía revista, citado en Otto Glasser's 1934 biography of Roentgen, aludes to these less scientific uses of x-ray photograph:

Los Rayos Roentgen, los Rayos Roentgen,

>

¿Qué es esta locura?

>

El incendio de la ciudad

>

√ Con la nueva fase

>

De las formas de rayos X.

Estoy lleno de daze,

>

- ¿Qué?

>

Para hoy

>

Oí que mirarán.

>

"Truco y vestido de Thro" e incluso se queda,

>

Estos traviesos y traviesos Rayos Roentgen.

Strandidyll A La Roentgen, 1900\. Postal Satórico de 1900 - media década después del descubrimiento de los rayos X, El Archivo de Internet.

Pero la fotografía y escena del arte es donde la creatividad (y la radiación) brillaron realmente. Dentro del primer año del descubrimiento de Röntgen, expertos influyentes de fotografía como Joseph Maria Eder ya estaban usando rayos Röntgen para crear imágenes exquisitas de muchos generalmente innardes invisibles, que van desde ranas y peces, hasta manos humanas o ornamentos. Estas imágenes se parecen a la fotografía de arte fino más que revistas médicas modernas y muestran las tendencias curiosas.

Versuche über Photographie mittelst der Röntgen'schen Strahlen (Experimentos en fotografía por medio de X-Rays), 1896, Joseph Maria Eder " Eduard Valenta, Public Domain Image Archive - El Museo Metropolitano.

La fotografía en sí misma ganaba su lugar como una forma de arte seria, más que sólo explotación técnica o forraje satírico, y los dos desarrollos iban de la mano al final de la era victoriana, evolucionando y a la vez influenciando el ojo público.

Otro científico interesado en jugar con el rayo, tan tarde como la década de 1930, fue el entusiasta de la fotografía Dr. Dain L. Tasker. Como osteopata de profesión y radiógrafo jefe en el Hospital Wilshire, el compromiso del Tasker con la radiografía podría presumir un interés médico. Sin embargo, los cientos de radiografías tomadas a lo largo de su carrera, en cambio, presentan flores como su principal fuente de inspiración.

Tulips: An X-ray (1931), The Snail (1930), Dahlia (1938) y Formosan Lily (1939) por el Dr. Dain L. Tasker. Todas las imágenes cortesía de Joseph Bellows GalleryLa Jolla, CA.

Al igual que Eder, el uso de la tecnología de rayos X sitúa esta etapa temprana del medio más allá en el territorio artístico con su serie de radiografías florales, un motivo más común en la pintura y la fotografía de la vida contemporánea que los hospitales. La radiografía parecía existir en su propio derecho artístico, independientemente de las esferas científicas del Dr. Tasker y el Dr. Röntgen.

¡No intentes esto en casa!

Sin embargo, el éxito temprano dramático de la fotografía de rayos X tenía su lado oscuro. A medida que la tendencia se desplomó, el peligro de la radiación se hizo difícil de ignorar, y rápidamente restringió la popularidad pública de los rayos X de DIY y cabinas radiográficas de estilo carnaval. Este extraño momento entre descubrimiento y comprensión dio lugar a las imágenes únicas que se presentan aquí, explotaciones artísticas que preferimos admirar desde una distancia más segura.

A medida que el mundo llegaba a darse cuenta del peligro que estaba causando esta radiografía sin filtrar, los recuerdos casuales de instantáneas de esqueleto rápidamente salieron de moda y los radiografos se limitaron a entornos clínicos controlados. Sin embargo, su influencia estética permaneció.

Con la radiografía cada vez más relegada al mundo médico, los movimientos modernos de fotografía seguían escaneando su legado para la inspiración visual. En 1921, Man Ray produjo una imagen curiosa sin cámara de contrastes y sombras, transparencia y opacidad, que dio la impresión de mirar a través de varias capas a la vez. Rayograph era una nueva mirada que barrió la escena del arte parisino por la tormenta... pero parece extrañamente familiar.

Crédito: Forms, Forms y The Manikin rayógrafos de Man Ray, Yale University Art Gallery, Regalo de Colección Société Anonyme.

El proceso de fotogramas no fue nuevo o exclusivo de la radiografía o el Rayograma, de hecho, datando todo el camino de regreso a los primeros dibujos fotogénicos de William Henry Fox Talbot a finales de los años 1830. Aunque Man Ray no reconoció ninguna inspiración directa de los radiografos de estilo Röntgen, sus creaciones y su interioridad se asemejaron fuertemente a la estética de la radiografía.

De hecho, muchos artistas en este momento en los años veinte recreaban miradas similares al rayógrafo. Era el contemporáneo de Man Ray, László Moholy-Nagy, quien reconoció explícitamente la influencia de los rayos X y la radiografía en su propio trabajo fotográfico. Sus fotogramas, con sus transluencias en capas blancas y negras, reflejaban de cerca la imagen radiográfica familiar en un estilo moderno adecuado para el siglo XX. x-ray photography:

“La pasión por las transparencias es una de las características más espectaculares de nuestro tiempo. En las fotos de rayos X, la estructura se convierte en transparencia y la transparencia manifiesta estructura. Las imágenes de rayos X, a las que el futurista se ha referido constantemente, se encuentran entre los notables renderizaciones espacio-tiempo en el plano estático”.

Además de las nuevas olas en los movimientos fotográficos, el siglo XX más tarde todavía vio un curioso uso contracultural de películas antiguas de rayos X fuera de los escenarios hospitalarios. El peligro de esta época era más político que basado en la salud – durante la censura de la Unión Soviética, surgió una escena subterránea para la robótica música occidental o prohibida.

Sin medios para producir discos de vinilo de forma extraoficial, surgió la idea de reutilizar imágenes de rayos X usadas de los hospitales locales como discos de música de contraband. Los discos de vinilo resultantes todavía mostraban las fotografías originales de rayos X, lo que llevó a la música que se conoce como Bones o Ribs!

Pyotr Leshchenko grabando en disco de película de rayos X, Wikimedia Commons y "Rock on Bones" registro, c. 1950s, Wikimedia Commons

El riesgo de las radiografías es una faceta fascinante de su historia cultural inusual y a menudo olvidada. Su peligro los removió permanentemente de manos públicas por el bien mayor, pero no sin pérdida a la fotografía experimental y el arte que inspiraron y facilitaron.

El X-Ray hoy

Con la transición de la radiografía de un exploit de entretenimiento personal sólidamente en el mundo médico, es un poco de vergüenza que la belleza de la radiografía como un instrumento para la fotografía experimental sea a menudo pasada por alto. Pero si usted está anhelando la visión artística de rayos X de los buenos viejos tiempos presalud y días de seguridad, no se preocupe! La fotografía de rayos X todavía está viva y bien hoy, con un riesgo considerablemente menos profesional que la historia de 1890

Para más información sobre el tema, consulte algunas de las fuentes siguientes:

  • Hospital General de Massachusetts
  • Historia de la gente del NHS
  • JSTOR Daily
  • Excillum
  • Iowa State University
  • El examen del dominio público

Para leer más sobre los lados inesperados de la historia de la fotografía, busque nuestra archival Magazine series o profundizar en el Joseph Petzval Archive. También puede compartir sus propias historias de fotos olvidadas con nosotros en [analoguearchive@lomography.com](mailto:analoguearchive@lomography.com).

Where was the last place you had an x-ray taken? In the twenty-first century the answer seems obvious: in hospital after a few broken bones. Rewind a hundred years, however, and you could find radiography, or x-ray photography, in some pretty strange places. The invention of radiography in 1895 quickly got under the general public’s skin, and became a form of photographic art and entertainment in its early days as much as a medical game-changer.

The instant explosion of radiographs into the everyday world was high risk, high reward since the dangers that came with this new technology initially went unnoticed and misunderstood. Never-before seen images of interiors inspired experimental photography and artwork, but also existential questions about life and death.

Murex inflatus (Riesenstachelschnecke), Röntgenaufnahme, Frtiz Block, 1931. X-ray image of real pearls (middle) and fake pearls (left and right), taken by Walter König at Physikalischer Verein, 1896. X-ray of a flower, extracted from The story of X-rays from Röntgen to Isotopes.png), 1960, Wikimedia Commons.

For a short period of its history, x-ray photography was in public hands before safety regulations and awareness changed, leaving us with some unique images which are unlikely to be recreated on the same scale in the modern world of photography.

Invention and Existentialism

“I have seen my death!”

This was the reaction to the world’s first ever human radiograph. Anna Bertha Röntgen, staring at an image of her own skeletal fingers and wedding ring (see below), was initially horrified by her husband’s discovery. Dr. Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, after weeks of experimentation, had just accidentally harnessed the power of unknown, or “X”, rays and tested them out on his unsuspecting wife.

Hand mit Ringen (Hand with Rings), Wilhelm Röntgen, 1896, Wikimedia Commons. A compass whose magnetic needle is entirely surrounded by metal, viewed through x-ray, W.K. von Röntgen, 1895, Wikimedia Commons. One block of glass, one of aluminium, two of calcite and two of quartz, viewed under x-ray, Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, 1895, Wikimedia Commons.

Transitioning from a fluorescent screen to photosensitive glass plates, he successfully captured the mysterious rays in a fixed image and began to investigate their properties. Besides photographing his wife’s hand, he experimented with metals and everyday objects. These initial photographs were used to share his new knowledge publicly.

The door of Röntgen's laboratory, with a platinum plate attached to the handle, viewed under x-ray. Photoprint from radiograph by W.K. von Röntgen, 1895. by Wilhelm Konrad von Röntgen - 1895 - Wellcome Collection, United Kingdom - CC BY.

The power of x-rays, or Röntgen rays as they are sometimes still called, was undeniable, and Dr. Röntgen soon generously made his discovery visible to society without patent due to their scientific value. Their medical use was of course a point of immediate interest, but x-ray photographs in the mid-1890s had a long way to go before becoming the specialized and exclusive medical practice they are today.

So, how much has this really got to do with photography?

Early X-ray Art: Flowers, Photography & Fun Fairs

The news of radiographs travelled far and wide very quickly, and radiographs were being recreated within months of Röntgen’s first announcement of the mystery rays' abilities. Following widespread public excitement about the phenomenon, soon came public x-ray demonstrations and interactive experiences.

Still unaware of the risks of radiation, it became possible to have x-ray photographs made of hands, heads, or bags during fairs and carnivals to take home as a souvenir. That’s right, no broken bones required – just endless exposure entertainment for the whole family! It was even possible to purchase DIY equipment to make your own radiograph images at home.

Glasgow's X-ray campaign against tuberculosis, 11th March-12th April, 1957, The Wellcome Collection. X-ray postcard advertisement.jpg), LMU's Werner Von Boltenstern collection, Wikimedia Commons.

X-rays showed up in many unusual places in the early twentieth century, including advertising, shoe stores, and cinema during what was considered a period of X-ray Mania. Similarly to the earlier trend of spirit photography, some people hoped that the x-ray could prove the existence of unseen entities, like spirits or the soul.

Not all public opinion was positive – there was plenty of concern and satire about the potential misuse of x-ray images, such as indecently looking into neighboring bodies beneath their clothes or nosying at the contents of someone's purse. Some people even believed that we would begin reading into one another's thoughts thanks to these mysterious, mischievous beams.

A satirical poem published in Photography magazine, quoted in Otto Glasser's 1934 biography of Roentgen, alludes to these less scientific uses of x-ray photography:

> The Roentgen Rays, the Roentgen Rays,

>

> What is this craze:

>

> The town's ablaze

>

> With the new phase

>

> Of X-ray's ways.

> I'm full of daze,

>

> Shock and amaze;

>

> For nowadays

>

> I hear they'll gaze

>

> Thro' cloak and gown -- and even stays,

>

> These naughty, naughty Roentgen Rays.

Strandidyll A La Roentgen, 1900\. Satirical postcard from 1900 - half a decade after the discovery of X-rays, The Internet Archive.

But the photography and art scene is where the creativity (and radiation) truly glowed. Within the first year of Röntgen’s discovery, influential photography experts like Joseph Maria Eder were already using Röntgen rays to create exquisite images of many usually unseen innards, ranging from frogs and fish, to human hands or ornaments. These images resemble fine art photography more than modern medical journals and show the curious overlap between art and science in the wake of new trends in photography and physics.

Versuche über Photographie mittelst der Röntgen'schen Strahlen (Experiments in Photography by means of X-Rays), 1896, Joseph Maria Eder & Eduard Valenta, Public Domain Image Archive / The Metropolitan Museum.

Photography itself was earning its place as a serious art form, more than just technical exploit or satirical fodder, and the two developments went hand in hand at the end of the Victorian era, evolving in and simultaneously influencing the public eye.

Another scientist keen to play with the ray, as late as the 1930s, was photography enthusiast Dr. Dain L. Tasker. As an osteopath by profession and chief radiographer at Wilshire Hospital, Tasker's engagement with the x-ray could be presumed a medical interest. However, the hundreds of radiographs taken throughout his career instead feature flowers as his primary source of inspiration.

Tulips: An X-ray (1931), The Snail (1930), Dahlia (1938) and Formosan Lily (1939) by Dr. Dain L. Tasker. All images courtesy of Joseph Bellows Gallery, La Jolla, CA.

Much like Eder, Tasker’s use of x-ray technology situates this early stage of the medium further into artistic territory with his series of floral radiographs — a motif more common in painting and contemporary still life photography than hospitals. The radiograph seemed to exist in its own artistic right, independently of the scientific spheres of Dr. Tasker and Dr. Röntgen.

Don’t try this at home!

The dramatic early success of x-ray photography had its dark side, however. As the trend swept over, the danger of the radiation became hard to ignore, and quickly curtailed the public popularity of DIY x-rays and carnival-style radiography booths. This strange moment between discovery and understanding resulted in the unique images featured here — artistic exploits we would now rather admire from a safer distance.

As the world came to realize the danger this unfiltered radiography was causing, the casual skeleton snapshot souvenirs quickly went out of fashion and radiographs were confined to controlled, clinical settings. However, their aesthetic influence remained.

With radiography becoming increasingly relegated to the medical world, modern photography movements were still scanning its legacy for visual inspiration. In 1921, Man Ray produced a curious camera-less image of contrasts and shadows, transparency and opaqueness, which gave the impression of looking through several layers at once. His Rayograph was a brand new look which swept the Parisian art scene by storm...yet it appears oddly familiar.

Credit: Forms, Forms and The Manikin rayographs by Man Ray, Yale University Art Gallery, Gift of Collection Société Anonyme.

The photogram process was not new or exclusive to the either the x-ray or the Rayogram, in fact, dating all the way back to William Henry Fox Talbot's first photogenic drawings in the late 1830s. Although Man Ray didn't acknowledge any direct inspiration from the Röntgen-style radiographs, his creations and their interiority strongly resembled the aesthetic of the x-ray.

Indeed, many artists at this time in the 1920s were recreating similar looks to the rayograph. It was Man Ray's contemporary, László Moholy-Nagy, who explicitly acknowledged the influence of x-rays and radiography on his own photographic work. His photograms, with their black and white layered translucencies, reflected closely the familiar radiographic image in a modern style fit for the twentieth century. Moholy-Nagy wrote about the contemporary relevance and cultural impact of x-ray photography:

> “The passion for transparencies is one of the most spectacular features of our time. In x-ray photos, structure becomes transparency and transparency manifests structure. The x-ray pictures, to which the futurist has consistently referred, are among the outstanding space-time renderings on the static plane.”

In addition to new waves in photography movements, the later twentieth century still saw some curious countercultural use of old x-ray films outside hospital settings. The danger this time was more political than health-based – during the censorship of the Soviet Union, an underground scene emerged for bootlegging Western or banned music.

With no means to produce vinyl albums unofficially, the idea emerged to repurpose used x-ray images from local hospitals as the discs for contraband music. The resulting vinyl albums still featured the original x-ray photographs, leading to the music being known as Bones or Ribs!

Pyotr Leshchenko recording on x-ray film disc, Wikimedia Commons and "Rock on Bones" record, c. 1950s, Wikimedia Commons

The risk of radiographs is a fascinating facet of their unusual and often forgotten cultural history. Their danger removed them permanently from public hands for the greater good, but not without loss to the experimental photography and art they inspired and facilitated.

The X-Ray Today

With the transition of radiography from a personal entertainment exploit solidly into the medical world, it's somewhat of a shame that the beauty of the x-ray as an instrument for experimental photography is often overlooked. But if you’re longing for the artsy x-ray vision of the good old pre-health and safety days, don’t fret! X-ray photography is still alive and well today, with considerably less professional risk than it involved in the 1890s. It might not be our first thought anymore when we hear the word “x-ray”, but the creative history behind the science still stands strong — if you look below the surface.

For further reading on the topic, consult some of the sources below:

  • Massachusetts General Hospital
  • People's History of the NHS
  • JSTOR Daily
  • Excillum
  • Iowa State University
  • The Public Domain Review

To read more about the unexpected sides of photography history, browse our archival Magazine series or delve into the Joseph Petzval Archive. You can also share your own forgotten photo stories with us at [analoguearchive@lomography.com](mailto:analoguearchive@lomography.com).

Con cada nueva adición a la línea de Lomography viene la misma pregunta irresistible: ¿qué revelarán los primeros rollos? El equipo de Lomography Vienna recientemente puso el nuevo Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera para probar y regresar con primeras impresiones, marcos favoritos y nuevos descubrimientos.

Tony – Abrazar Diptychs no planificados

¿Cuáles fueron sus primeras impresiones cuando usted tuvo la cámara de película de uso simple de medio marco y lo demuestran para una sesión?

Lo primero que me vino a la mente fue cómo se sentía la luz. Estoy constantemente filmando con cámaras de punto y disparo, y son notablemente más pesados. El tamaño se sentía justo en mis manos, y tenía un agarre cómodo mientras lo utilizaba.

  • !Image 1
  • !Image 2
  • !Image 3

Créditos: Tony Sotelo TENIDO Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera LomoChrome Classicolor

Su primer vuelco cuenta con algunos grandes diptychs. ¿Cómo se acercaron a disparar estos, y qué la cámara fotográfica a la experiencia?

Al principio, traté de crear imágenes que trabajarían juntos como pares, manteniendo el diptych final en mente antes de presionar el obturador. Me acerqué a cada disparo muy deliberadamente, pero teniendo tantos marcos completamente cambiaron la forma en que filmé. En algún momento, naturalmente pierdes la pista de lo que has fotografiado, y eso me hizo dejar ir de intentar controlar la secuencia final. En lugar, comencé a experimentar más con cada cuadro sólo para adaptarse el filtro de flash.

Créditos: Tony Sotelo TENIDO Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera LomoChrome Classicolor

Cuéntanos sobre tu pareja de imágenes favorita. ¿Qué te hace especial?

Este es uno de mis diptych favoritos porque el uso de diferentes colores flash cambia completamente el estado de ánimo de una imagen. Me encanta este par porque elegí dos colores diferentes que todavía funcionan bien juntos y crear una conversación entre las imágenes. También es especial para mí porque fue uno de los primeros diptychs donde dejé de pensar y simplemente dejar que las cosas sucedan.

Disparaste con cámaras LomoChrome Classicolor y Black y White. ¿Cómo se adaptó la cámara a cada película?

Ya sea que estés filmando color o blanco y negro, la cámara tiene la misma sensación general. Con la película precargada de Lady Grey B plagaW ISO 400, me sentí un tiro un poco más seguro en situaciones de poca luz. Naturalmente me encontré prestando más atención a la luz y la sombra, buscando escenas con fuerte contraste y formas definidas. La cámara manejaba la gama tonal de manera hermosa, y estaba muy feliz con los resultados.

  • !Image 5
  • !Image 6

Créditos: Lomography Vienna Silencio Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White

Francesco – La calidez floral de los exteriores

¿Dónde trajiste la cámara de película recargable de uso simple de medio marco, y qué temas acabas fotografiando?

Lo traje a varios lugares por Viena y Budapest. Tuve la fortuna de poder usar la cámara durante una semana increíblemente sucesiva. Dos fotos retratan Budapest: en el primero, estoy sentado bajo los arcos de la Basción del Pescador, mientras que la segunda foto muestra las flores de naranja en los jardines de la Plaza de la Libertad. El resto de las fotos fueron disparadas en Viena: Burggarten, Stadtpark, y Schönbrunery - un montón de fotos

¿Cómo complementó el LomoChrome Classicolor las imágenes que capturaste usando la cámara?

Añadió mucha profundidad y, sobre todo para las fotos tomadas por la noche, creó algunos bonitos juegos de luz. También disfruto de la atmósfera analógica vintage que crean.

  • !Image 7
  • !Image 8
  • !Image 9
  • !Image 10

Créditos: Francesco Santangelo TENIDO Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera LomoChrome Classicolor

Después de pasar algún tiempo con él, ¿qué tipo de escenas o ocasiones crees que esta cámara de 35 mm de media cámara es la mejor opción?

Creo que es ideal para representar situaciones dinámicas en las que están involucrados personas o acciones. Si quisiera disparar paisajes, optaría por una cámara enmarcada regularmente. Si la acción está involucrada, preferiría una cámara de medio marco. No sólo permite que usted tome el doble de la cantidad de imágenes, pero también puede crear un diptych de dos tomas complementarias que mejora la narración, como lo intenté en mis tomas de Claudio y las rosas.

Antonia – Cuando la música se reúne con el monocromo

Muchas de sus imágenes se sienten espontáneas y energéticas. ¿Cómo se realizó la cámara de película de uso simple de medio marco para capturar escenas de bastón?

Decidí llevarlo a una erupción al aire libre en Viena. Considerando que saltamos un poco y seguimos yendo hacia atrás y hacia adelante entre el escenario, la cámara era perfecta para tomar fotos ya que es tan fácil de llevar. La mayoría lo sostenía en mi mano, o dentro de mi bolsillo, y decidí disparar cuando me sentía así.

  • !Image 11
  • !Image 12
  • !Image 13
  • !Image 14
  • !Image 15

Créditos: Antonia Klengel Silencio Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White

¿Cómo la cámara y la Dama Grey B PulW trabajaron juntos en tus imágenes? ¿Qué crees que disparar en monocromo se suma a la sensación general de tus fotos?

Era escéptico sobre la película negra y blanca al principio porque normalmente opto por el color, y era un día tan soleado que se sentía como un desperdicio al principio. Pero me sorprendió mucho los resultados, y siento que la película blanca y negra se adapta perfectamente al ambiente de ese lugar.

Rodrigo – Retratos bajo la luz cambiante

¿Qué te sorprendió más cuando obsequia los resultados de tu primer vuelco?

Me sorprendió que la lente capturara el ambiente que estaba persiguiendo. Se adapta bien a muchas situaciones – especialmente contextos casuales y urbanos. También me impresionó que podría conseguir muchas imágenes. Usando un medio marco realmente le permite no estresar o sobrepensar cuántas imágenes has dejado y concentrarme en capturar el momento.

  • !Image 16
  • !Image 17
  • !Image 18
  • !Image 19

Créditos: Rodrigo Toledo TENIDO Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera LomoChrome Classicolor

¿Cómo se mantuvo la cámara de película recargable de uso simple de medio marco bajo diferentes condiciones de tiro?

La cámara es extremadamente versátil. Ya que la cámara incluye un gel flash y flash, usted puede explorar diferentes resultados. Personalmente, me gusta los resultados con flash – su carga de tiempo es muy rápida, que me encanta porque asegura un buen resultado en situaciones de ritmo rápido. Era el tamaño que lo hizo el compañero perfecto para cada situación. Se mezcla bien al aire libre y no abruma a nadie delante de ella. Esto permitió que todos los involucrados en las sesiones se

De todas las fotos que ha tomado, ¿qué marco te destaca más, y por qué?

Mi favorito personal es este. Creo que es porque te dice mucho sobre el personaje sin ver su cara. Su piel te cuenta sobre un pasado y la forma en que se está cubriendo no mirando la cámara sugiere un regalo íntimo.

Créditos: Rodrigo Toledo TENIDO Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera LomoChrome Classicolor

Melissa – En el calor del verano

Sus primeros vuelcos están llenos de soleadas escenas al aire libre. ¿A dónde viajar y cuál fue el punto culminante de su viaje?

Estas fotos fueron tomadas durante mis recientes escapadas de fin de semana al sur de Portugal, Turquía y la región de Piamonte de Italia. Cada lugar tiene sus propios recuerdos únicos: las hermosas calas del sur de Portugal, las vibraciones pacíficas y gente super amigable del pueblo de Karaöz en la provincia de Antalya de Turquía, y las idílicas colinas de Monferrato con sus viñedos enrollados.

  • !Image 21
  • !Image 22
  • !Image 23

Créditos: Melissa Peritore Silencio Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera LomoChrome Classicolor

¿Qué te gustó más acerca de tomar la cámara de película de uso simple de medio marco con usted?

Me encanta cómo encaja fácilmente en un paquete o un bolsillo, lo que significa que siempre puedo tenerlo en mí – es tan fácil llevarlo por todas partes. Ser capaz de disparar el doble de los marcos en un solo rollo también hace que sea increíblemente conveniente!

Es tu turno de tomar el Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera No te olvides de compartir donde lo estás tomando, qué temas vas a estar filmando, y qué papel de película planeas emparejarlo en los comentarios de abajo!

With every new addition to the Lomography lineup comes the same irresistible question: what will the first rolls reveal? The Lomography Vienna team recently put the new Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera to test and returned with first impressions, favorite frames, and new discoveries.

Tony – Embracing Unplanned Diptychs

What were your first impressions when you first held the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera and took it out for a shoot?

The first thing that came to my mind was how light it felt. I’m constantly shooting with point-and-shoot cameras, and they’re noticeably heavier. The size felt just right in my hands, and I had a comfortable grip while using it.

  • !Image 1
  • !Image 2
  • !Image 3

Credits: Tony Sotelo | Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera LomoChrome Classicolor

Your first roll features some great diptychs. How did you approach shooting these, and what did the camera add to the experience?

At first, I tried to create images that would work together as pairs, keeping the final diptych in mind before pressing the shutter. I approached each shot very deliberately, but having so many frames completely changed the way I shot. At some point, you naturally lose track of what you've photographed, and that made me let go of trying to control the final sequence. Instead, I started experimenting more with each frame just for the fun of it. I played around with the flash and the color filters, mixing flash and natural light, exploring different color combinations, and photographing a variety of scenes to see just how adaptable the camera could be.

Credits: Tony Sotelo | Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera LomoChrome Classicolor

Tell us about your favorite image pair. What makes it special to you?

This is one of my favorite diptychs because using different flash colors completely changes the mood of an image. I love this pair because I chose two different colors that still work beautifully together and create a conversation between the images. It’s also special to me because it was one of the first diptychs where I stopped overthinking and just let things happen.

You shot with both LomoChrome Classicolor and Black and White cameras. How did the camera adapt to each film?

Whether you're shooting color or black and white, the camera has the same overall feel. With the preloaded Lady Grey B&W ISO 400 film, I felt a bit more confident shooting in lower-light situations. I naturally found myself paying more attention to light and shadow, looking for scenes with strong contrast and defined shapes. The camera handled the tonal range beautifully, and I was really happy with the results.

  • !Image 5
  • !Image 6

Credits: Lomography Vienna | Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White

Francesco – Floral Warmth of the Outdoors

Where did you bring the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera, and what subjects did you end up photographing?

I brought it to several places across Vienna and Budapest. I had the fortune of being able to use the camera during an incredibly eventful week. Two photos portray Budapest: in the first, I am sitting under the arches of the Fisherman's Bastion, while the second photo depicts the orange flowers in the gardens of Liberty Square. The rest of the photos were shot in Vienna: Burggarten, Stadtpark, and Schönbrunn – a lot of greenery. In the photos, you can see my two friends Claudio and Martina, who came to visit me during the weekend.

How did the LomoChrome Classicolor complement the images you captured using the camera?

It added a lot of depth and, especially for photos taken at night, created some nice plays of light. I also enjoy the vintage analogue atmosphere they create.

  • !Image 7
  • !Image 8
  • !Image 9
  • !Image 10

Credits: Francesco Santangelo | Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera LomoChrome Classicolor

After spending some time with it, what kinds of scenes or occasions do you think this 35 mm half-frame film camera is best suited for?

I think it’s ideal in representing dynamic situations where people or actions are involved. If I wanted to shoot landscapes, I would opt for a regularly framed camera. If action is involved, I would prefer a half-frame camera. Not only does it allow you to take double the amount of pictures, but it can also create a diptych of two complementary shots that enhances storytelling, as I attempted to do in my shots of Claudio and the roses.

Antonia – When Music Meets Monochrome

Many of your images feel spontaneous and energetic. How did the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera perform when capturing candid scenes?

I decided to take it to an outdoor rave in Vienna. Considering that we jumped around quite a bit and kept going back and forth between the stage, the camera was perfect for taking pictures as it’s so easy to carry around. I mostly just held it in my hand, or inside my pocket, and decided to shoot whenever I felt like it.

  • !Image 11
  • !Image 12
  • !Image 13
  • !Image 14
  • !Image 15

Credits: Antonia Klengel | Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White

How did the camera and the Lady Grey B&W work together in your images? What do you think shooting in monochrome added to the overall feel of your photos?

I was skeptical about the black and white film at first because I usually opt for color, and it was such a sunny day that it felt like a waste at first. But I was really surprised by the results, and I feel like the black and white film perfectly suits the vibe of that venue.

Rodrigo – Portraits Under Changing Light

What surprised you most when you got the results from your first roll?

I was surprised that the lens captured the vibe that I was pursuing. It adapts well to many situations – especially casual and urban contexts. I was also impressed that I could get that many pictures. Using a half-frame really allows you to not stress or overthink how many pictures you have left and focus on capturing the moment.

  • !Image 16
  • !Image 17
  • !Image 18
  • !Image 19

Credits: Rodrigo Toledo | Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera LomoChrome Classicolor

How did the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera hold up under different shooting conditions?

The camera is extremely versatile. Since the camera includes a flash and flash gels, you can explore different outcomes. Personally, I like the results with flash – its time charge is really quick, which I love because it ensures a nice result in fast paced situations. It was the size that made it the perfect companion for every situation. It blends well outdoors and it doesn't overwhelm anyone in front of it. This allowed everyone involved in the shoots to relax and show their honest selves.

Out of all the photos you’ve taken, which frame stands out to you the most, and why?

My personal favourite is this one. I think it's because it tells you so much about the character without seeing his face. His skin tells you about a past and the way he's covering himself not looking at the camera suggests an intimate present.

Credits: Rodrigo Toledo | Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera LomoChrome Classicolor

Melissa – In the Heat of Summer

Your first rolls are filled with sunny outdoor scenes. Where did you travel to and what was the highlight of your trip?

These photos were taken during my recent long weekend getaways to the south of Portugal, Turkey, and Italy's Piedmont region. Each place has its own unique memories: the beautiful coves of southern Portugal, the peaceful vibes and super friendly people of Karaöz village in the Antalya province of Turkey, and the idyllic Monferrato hills with their rolling vineyards.

  • !Image 21
  • !Image 22
  • !Image 23

Credits: Melissa Peritore | Shot with the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera LomoChrome Classicolor

What did you enjoy most about taking the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera with you?

I love how it easily fits right into a fanny pack or pocket, meaning I can always have it on me – it's so effortless to carry it everywhere. Being able to shoot double the frames on a single roll also makes it incredibly convenient!

It's your turn to take the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera for a spin. Don't forget to share where you're taking it, what subjects will you be shooting, and what film stock you plan to pair it with in the comments below!
