In this feature, we catch up with portrait photographer Green, also known as midori.pix), who recently put the Lomo MC-A to the test across two portrait sessions in completely different settings. Join us as he shares his experience with the camera, his thoughts after shooting with it, and, of course, the photographs that came out of the experience.

© midori.pix

Hi, Green! Could you briefly introduce yourself and tell us how you got into photography?

Hello everyone! I'm Green, a.k.a midori.pix, a portrait and graduation photographer. My style leans toward warm, soft, nostalgic images with the timeless feel of classic film photography. My journey into photography began when my older brother gave me a camera and a few lenses to experiment with. From there, I started exploring different genres of photography, and before I knew it, more than ten years had passed.

About five years ago, I discovered the unique charm of vintage film colors and classic film stocks. I was drawn to their distinctive look and the creative challenge they offered. Since then, I've been shooting film consistently because I want every graduation portrait and profile photo I take to feel a little different, carrying the nostalgic atmosphere and timeless character of traditional film photography.

© midori.pix | Camera: Lomo MC-A | Film: LomoChrome Classicolor ISO 200 | Model: dinipts

What was your first impression of the Lomo MC-A? And after spending some time shooting with it, how would you describe its character?

My first impression was that it's incredibly compact, charming, and has a classic look. It immediately gave me the feel of a point-and-shoot camera, small enough to slip into a shirt pocket and easy to carry anywhere. But once I actually started shooting with it, I realized it has a character I'd describe as “raw, yet beautifully balanced.” The colors are rich and vibrant, with subtle vignetting around the edges that gives images that unmistakable Lomography look.

What really surprised me, though, was how beautifully it renders portraits in natural light. Skin tones come out soft and smooth without looking harsh at all. For such a compact camera, it also packs in some fun creative features, like double exposure, which makes it perfect for anyone who enjoys experimenting with more expressive, artistic photographs.

© midori.pix | Camera: Lomo MC-A | Film: LomoChrome Classicolor ISO 200 | Model: dinipts

Where did you take the Lomo MC-A, and what did you choose to photograph?

I actually took the MC-A out for two separate portrait sessions in two completely different locations, each with its own atmosphere and a different model, so the results had a very distinct feel.

The first shoot was in Talad Noi. I took my model on a relaxed street portrait walk through the neighborhood's narrow alleyways and old buildings. It was all about strolling around, camera in hand, waiting for the right moments and shooting naturally. I focused on capturing the afternoon sunlight as it spilled across weathered concrete walls and vintage cars. The camera's character complemented the location perfectly, giving the images a raw, vintage aesthetic that really enhanced the mood of the surroundings.

© midori.pix | Camera: Lomo MC-A | Film: LomoChrome Classicolor ISO 200 | Model: dinipts

The second session took place at the Chatuchak Fish Market. This time, I wanted to experiment with indoor lighting and a completely different atmosphere. I captured candid moments of another model quietly admiring the aquariums, with the neon lights and reflections from the glass tanks falling across her face. The Lomo MC-A rendered those layers of light beautifully, giving the images a soft, mysterious, and almost cinematic quality.

Across both shoots, my approach was the same: keep everything spontaneous and embrace a true point-and-shoot mindset. I didn't rely on any elaborate techniques or complicated setups, just the camera, the moment, and whatever unfolded naturally in front of me.

© midori.pix | Camera: Lomo MC-A | Film: Lomography Color Negative ISO 400 | Model: linnpingg__

The Lomo MC-A comes with Auto, Aperture Priority, and Manual shooting modes. Do you think having this level of control makes the camera easier to use?

Absolutely. It makes shooting both easier and a lot more enjoyable. When you're out walking with a camera, the light is constantly changing. On days when I just want to raise the camera and capture the moment, I simply switch to Auto or Aperture Priority mode. I can open up the aperture for a beautifully soft background, let the camera handle the rest, and confidently catch those spontaneous, unplanned moments.

“The camera's character complemented the location perfectly, giving the images a raw, vintage aesthetic that really enhanced the mood of the surroundings.”

But when I step into a darker alley or want to create a dramatic backlit silhouette, I can easily switch to Manual mode and dial everything in myself. That flexibility means the MC-A can adapt to almost any shooting style or creative idea, which is something I really appreciate.

© midori.pix | Camera: Lomo MC-A | Film: Lomography Color Negative ISO 400 | Model: linnpingg__

The Lomo MC-A features Autofocus, Manual Zone Focus, manual ISO settings, and easy-to-use Exposure Compensation. Do you prefer controlling everything yourself, or do you usually let the camera take over?

I'd say it's more like the camera and I share the creative process, though we occasionally have our disagreements. One thing I almost always like to control myself is Exposure Compensation, because I prefer my images to be slightly underexposed. It gives them the moody, melancholic atmosphere that's become part of my style.

As for the autofocus, it's genuinely smart and performs just as you'd expect from a modern point-and-shoot. That said, it does have its stubborn moments. In very low light or when the background is particularly busy, the camera sometimes seems to hesitate, almost as if it's asking itself, “Wait...what should I focus on?” The shutter locks, and no matter how many times I press it, it simply refuses to take the shot.

When that happens, I just switch over to Manual Zone Focus and take control myself. Honestly, I don't mind it at all – it adds a bit of personality to the experience. Those quirky moments keep you engaged and remind you that you're interacting with a camera, not just pressing a button.

© midori.pix | Camera: Lomo MC-A | Film: Lomography Color Negative ISO 400 | Model: linnpingg__

What was your reaction when you saw the results for the first time?

“That's the film look!” Point-and-shoot, simply as that! The images look very lively. The lens delivers beautiful colors, retains plenty of detail, and produces images with balanced contrast and smooth tonal transitions. There is a touch of the crispness you'd expect from a compact camera, but it still feels very natural.

With a maximum shutter speed of 1/500, you'll sometimes want to shoot with a wider aperture, but that's never really an issue. What impressed me most, though, was the camera's metering. Whether I was shooting into the light, using flash, or relying solely on available light, the exposure was consistently accurate. It handled backlit scenes especially well, giving me exactly the results I was hoping for.

© midori.pix | Camera: Lomo MC-A | Film: Lomography Color Negative ISO 400 | Model: linnpingg__

What kinds of situations or occasions is the Lomo MC-A best suited for?

I'd say it's at its best from around 4 p.m. through sunset. The light during those hours is simply beautiful, and it's hard to take a bad photo. It's also the perfect camera to keep with you as an everyday companion, whether you're wandering around on a day off, café hopping, or spending time with friends during a graduation pre-shoot.

It's also a lot of fun to experiment with Double Exposure. You can pass the camera around, take turns composing and shooting, and create something together without worrying about getting everything technically perfect. The result is a collection of photographs that feel stylish, full of character, and unlike anyone else's.

© midori.pix | Camera: Lomo MC-A | Film: Lomography Color Negative ISO 400 | Model: linnpingg__

If you were to take the Lomo MC-A out for another photo walk, what song would you choose as the soundtrack for the day?

I'd go with Plastic Love by Mariya Takeuchi. It's a classic Japanese city pop track from the '80s with a funky groove, but there's a subtle sense of melancholy beneath it. That combination perfectly complements the Lomo MC-A's vibrant colors and vintage character. Put on that song, wander around with the camera, and keep pressing the shutter. You'll be so immersed in the experience that you'll lose track of time.

Do you have any advice for people who are interested in trying the Lomo MC-A for themselves?

I’d say, “Relax and just enjoy the process.” This camera wasn’t made to produce perfectly sharp images like the latest smartphones. Some photos might come out blurry, or you might accidentally create a double exposure that leaves you wondering what happened, but that’s exactly where the charm and creativity of point-and-shoot film photography come from.

Allow yourself to experiment, make mistakes, and discover what the camera can do. Once you embrace that process, you’ll start to appreciate and fall in love with this unique kind of photographic experience.

© midori.pix | Camera: Lomo MC-A | Film: Lomography Color Negative ISO 400 | Model: linnpingg__

For anyone who’s preparing for a graduation shoot or looking for a photographer to capture stylish film-inspired portraits with a warm and natural mood, feel free to check out my work, have a chat, ask for advice, or inquire about availability through my Instagram: midori.pix.

A huge thank you to Green for sharing his experience with the Lomo MC-A with us. The photographs he created are truly stunning and showcase the camera’s unique character so beautifully. Stay tuned to see who we’ll be interviewing next!

Ishmael Claxton es un fotógrafo afroamericano residente en Dublín (Irlanda) que ha sabido aprovechar los diversos tonos y matices de las películas LomoChrome para expresar diferentes ideas en torno a la raza, la identidad y el significado. Una de sus series, Garden of Eden (Jardín del Edén), emplea la película LomoChrome Purple de 35 mm ISO 100–400 para documentar la juventud y los momentos de transición.

Por otro lado, en su proyecto reciente Dead Zoo in Blue, fotografió el laboratorio del «Zoo Muerto» en el Museo Nacional de Irlanda, capturando todo el trabajo con la película LomoChrome Turquoise de 35 mm ISO 100–400. La obra plantea interrogantes sobre la descolonización dentro de los espacios museísticos, con un especial hincapié en el desmantelamiento del Zoo Muerto. Hablamos con Ishmael sobre su labor, los mensajes que busca transmitir a través de su práctica y las razones por las que elige disparar con películas LomoChrome.

Fotografías de Ishmael Claxton | Tomadas con LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100–400

Hola, Ishmael, ¿podrías hablarnos un poco sobre ti?

Soy un artista visual y fotógrafo afincado en Dublín. Creví en la ciudad de Nueva York durante los años noventa y principios de los 2000, en un barrio que primero se vio duramente golpeado por las drogas y más tarde por oleadas de gentrificación. Ver un lugar cambiar con tanta rapidez moldeó mi forma de entender las imágenes, la memoria y quiénes siguen siendo visibles a medida que las ciudades se transforman.

Mi trabajo oscila entre la fotografía, la instalación y la curadoría colaborativa. Fotografío a personas, espacios y objetos que ya portan historias propias. Una exposición en un museo, la esquina de una calle o un retrato íntimo pueden revelar vestigios de poder, migración y pertenencia. La fotografía se convirtió en el medio a través del cual ordeno esas capas. A menudo mezclo imágenes preparadas con instantes documentales porque la vida real rara vez encaja de forma pulcida en una sola categoría.

Fotografías de Ishmael Claxton | Tomadas con LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100–400

En los últimos años, mi trabajo ha sido reconocido con diversos premios y exposiciones. En 2023, fui seleccionado como finalista en los LensCulture Editors’ Pick. En 2024, mi obra fue preseleccionada tanto para el Taylor Wessing Photographic Portrait Prize como para la Royal Photographic Society International Photography Exhibition 166. En 2025, fui elegido como uno de los 100 fotógrafos de Bellas Artes del mañana para la exposición Shutter Hub OPEN en la Universidad de Cambridge.

Mi obra se ha exhibido en espacios como el Museum of Literature Ireland, el PhotoMuseum Ireland, la Sala Nacional de Conciertos (National Concert Hall), la Exposición Anual de la RHA, el Hunt Museum, la Royal Ulster Academy, la Irish Georgian Society, Russborough House y la Gallery X. También he participado en residencias que han contribuido a consolidar mi práctica, entre ellas PhotoMuseum Ireland, el Center for Visual Storytelling en Santa Fe, Cow House Studios, 3 Walls Gallery, la residencia de otoño de Culture Vulture y Queens Collective. Asimismo, soy cofundador de ÍOVA Collective, un grupo impulsado por fotógrafos en Irlanda que apoya a los creadores de imágenes y genera espacios para propuestas inéditas.

Fotografías de Ishmael Claxton

¿Cómo te iniciaste en la fotografía analógica?

Tuve mi primer contacto con la película en un taller extraescolar cuando cursaba la educación secundaria básica. Teníamos un pequeño laboratorio y recuerdo haber visto cómo una imagen aparecía lentamente en la cubeta de revelado. Aquel momento se quedó grabado en mí. Años más tarde, volví al celuloide tras dos sucesos ocurridos en poco tiempo. Un disco duro digital falló y perdí años de imágenes. Poco después, la casa de mis padres se incendió. Las únicas fotografías que sobrevivieron a ambas desgracias fueron los negativos y las copias en papel.

“El color es una de mis herramientas favoritas en la fotografía. Cambiar el tipo de película puede transformar por completo nuestra forma de ver el mundo”.

Esa experiencia alteró mi perspectiva sobre la fotografía. La película perdura. Permanece en silencio dentro de una caja esperando a que la busques. De regreso en Nueva York, comencé a tomar clases en el Bushwick Community Darkroom, donde tuve como mentora a Lucia Rollow. Aquella etapa en el cuarto oscuro me infundió un respeto más profundo por el oficio y por la paciencia que exige la fotografía química. Desde entonces, confío en ella de otra manera.

Fotografías de Ishmael Claxton | Tomadas con LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100–400

Háblanos de este proyecto y de cómo surgió.

Trabajo con frecuencia con emulsiones de Lomography porque sus virajes de color transportan la imagen hacia rumbos inesperados. La película misma pasa a formar parte del lenguaje de la obra. Para una serie titulada Garden of Eden en tonos púrpuras, utilicé película con matices morados para fotografiar la cultura juvenil y los momentos de transición. También empleé LomoChrome Metropolis para documentar viviendas en ruinas y edificios vacíos durante la crisis inmobiliaria.

El color es capaz de transmitir significado incluso antes de que el espectador lea la fotografía. En el caso de los retratos *queer*, recurrí de nuevo al púrpura porque concentra al mismo tiempo delicadeza y tensión. Con los tonos turquesa y azul comencé a desarrollar proyectos como Dead Zoo in Blue y Mood Indigo. Estas obras transitan por museos, archivos y retratos para cuestionar de qué modo la raza, la identidad y los cuerpos han sido clasificados o exhibidos en el interior de las instituciones.

Serie Garden of Eden por Ishmael Claxton | Tomada con LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100–400

¿Qué te motivó a fotografiar el proyecto Dead Zoo in Blue empleando exclusivamente la película LomoChrome Turquoise?

El color es una de mis herramientas favoritas en la fotografía. Cambiar el tipo de película puede transformar por completo nuestra forma de ver el mundo. La película turquesa altera los colores justo lo necesario para que las escenas cotidianas parezcan ligeramente extrañas. Los tonos de piel, los cielos y las sombras se alejan de lo que damos por sentado. Ese desplazamiento me resulta útil; interrumpe nuestros hábitos visuales. Cuando todo un conjunto de obras se realiza bajo la misma paleta, adquiere su propia atmósfera y el espectador se adentra de lleno en ese universo.

La mayor parte de la película de Lomography que utilizo proviene de la John Gunn Camera Shop. La familia Gunn se ha convertido en una parte fundamental de la comunidad fotográfica en Dublín. Hace unos años, les pregunté si considerarían la posibilidad de tener película de Lomography en stock. La trajeron y, desde entonces, más fotógrafos de por aquí han empezado a experimentar con ella. Ha sido gratificante comprobar cómo ese pequeño cambio ha contribuido a hacer crecer la comunidad analógica local.

Ishmael Claxton is an African-American photographer now based in Dublin, Ireland who has been utilizing the various tones and hues from LomoChrome films to express different ideas on race, identity and meaning. One of his series, Garden of Eden, uses LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100–400 film to document youth and moments of transition.

Meanwhile, in a recent project, Dead Zoo in Blue, he photographed the Dead Zoo Lab at The National Museum of Ireland and shot the entire project on LomoChrome Turquoise 35 mm ISO 100–400 35 mm film. The work raises questions about decolonization within museum spaces, with a special focus on the dismantling of the Dead Zoo. We talked to Ishmael about his work, the messages he wants to create through his practice and and why he chooses to shoot with LomoChrome films.

Photos by Ishmael Claxton | Shot with the LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100–400

Hi Ishmael, please tell us a bit about yourself?

I am a visual artist and photographer based in Dublin. I grew up in New York City in the 1990s and early 2000s, in a neighborhood that was first hit by drugs and later by waves of gentrification. Watching a place change that quickly shaped how I think about images, memory, and who gets to remain visible as cities transform.

My work moves between photography, installation, and curating with others. I photograph people, spaces, and objects that already carry histories. A museum display, a street corner, or a quiet portrait can all reveal traces of power, migration, and belonging. Photography became the way I sort through those layers. I often mix staged images with documentary moments because real life rarely sits neatly in one category.

Photos by Ishmael Claxton | Shot with the LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100–400

Over the past few years my work has been recognized through several awards and exhibitions. In 2023, I was shortlisted for the LensCulture Editors’ Pick. In 2024, my work was shortlisted for both the Taylor Wessing Photographic Portrait Prize and the Royal Photographic Society International Photography Exhibition 166. In 2025, I was selected as one of the 100 Fine Art Photographers of Tomorrow for the Shutter Hub OPEN exhibition at the University of Cambridge.

My work has been shown at places including the Museum of Literature Ireland, PhotoMuseum Ireland, the National Concert Hall, the RHA Annual Exhibition, the Hunt Museum, the Royal Ulster Academy, the Irish Georgian Society, Russborough House, and Gallery X. I have also taken part in residencies that helped shape my practice, including PhotoMuseum Ireland, the Center for Visual Storytelling in Santa Fe, Cow House Studios, 3 Walls Gallery, Culture Vulture Autumn AIR, and Queens Collective. I am also a co-founder of ÍOVA Collective, a photographer-led group in Ireland that supports image makers and creates space for new work.

Photos by Ishmael Claxton

How did you get into shooting film?

I first touched film in an after school program when I was in junior high school. We had a small darkroom and I remember watching an image slowly appear in the developer tray. That moment stayed with me. Years later, I came back to film after two events happened close together. A digital hard drive crashed and I lost years of images. Not long after that, my family home burned down. The only photographs that survived both events were negatives and prints.

“Color is one of my favorite tools in photography. Changing the film stock can completely shift how we see the world.”

That experience changed the way I thought about photography. Film lasts. It sits quietly in a box and waits for you. When I returned to New York, I started taking classes at the Bushwick Community Darkroom, where I was mentored by Lucia Rollow. That time in the darkroom gave me a deeper respect for the craft and the patience film demands. Since then, I have trusted it in a different way.

Photos by Ishmael Claxton | Shot with the LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100–400

Tell us about this project and how it came about?

I often work with Lomography film stocks because their color shifts push the image somewhere unexpected. The film itself becomes part of the language of the work. For a series called Garden of Eden in Purple, I used purple-toned film to photograph youth culture and moments of transition. I also used LomoChrome Metropolis to photograph crumbling housing and empty buildings during the housing crisis.

Color can carry meaning before a viewer even reads the photograph. For queer portraits, I leaned into purple again because it holds softness and tension at the same time. With turquoise and blue tones I began developing projects like Dead Zoo in Blue and Mood Indigo. These works move through museums, archives, and portraiture to question how race, identity, and bodies have been classified or displayed inside institutions.

Garden of Eden Series by Ishmael Claxton | Shot with the LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100–400

What made you want to shoot the Dead Zoo in Blue project using only LomoChrome Turquoise film?

Color is one of my favorite tools in photography. Changing the film stock can completely shift how we see the world. Turquoise film bends color just enough to make familiar scenes feel slightly strange. Skin tones, skies, and shadows all move away from what we expect. That shift is useful to me. It interrupts our habits of looking. When an entire body of work is made with the same palette, it builds its own atmosphere and the viewer steps into that world.

Most of the Lomography film I use comes from John Gunn Camera Shop. The Gunn’s family have become an important part of the photography community in Dublin. A few years ago, I actually asked if they would consider stocking Lomography film. They brought it in, and since then more photographers here have started experimenting with it. It has been nice to see that small shift help grow a local film community.

Photos by Ishmael Claxton | Shot with the LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100–400

If the LomoChrome Turquoise film you used for your project, Dead Zoo in Blue, had a soundtrack, what song would capture its mood best?

When I look at those colors, I hear jazz. The first song that comes to mind is Mood Indigo by Duke Ellington. I also think of the quiet intensity of Nina Simone and the spiritual depth of Alice Coltrane. Those sounds carry blue in the same way the film does. Slow, reflective, and full of feeling.

Garden of Eden Series by Ishmael Claxton | Shot with the LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100–400

What’s coming up for you in 2026?

2026 has already been an incredibly rewarding year and many of the projects I began developing over the last few years have finally taken shape. One of the biggest has been Mood Indigo, an ongoing portrait series inspired by the Irish phrase “duine gorm”, a historical term once used to describe Black people that literally translates as blue person”. Originally conceived as a series of 100 portraits, I decided to expand the project to 120 portraits, marking each year of Irish independence and allowing the work to continue growing beyond a fixed endpoint. Using specialized blue tinted film, the project explores identity, belonging, and contemporary Black life in Ireland.

As of August 2026, I have photographed 118 people of color from across Ireland, ranging in age from 6 to 85 years old. The project has introduced me to extraordinary individuals from a wide range of backgrounds and experiences, and those conversations have become just as important as the photographs themselves. I am excited to see where the final portraits, and the relationships formed through the project, will lead in the years ahead.

Earlier this year, I also released Dead Zoo in Blue, a project that began during my African Artist Residency at Photo Museum Ireland in collaboration with the National Museum of Ireland – Natural History. The work examines museum collections through the lens of colonial history, asking how bodies, objects, and narratives have been classified, preserved, and interpreted over time. The accompanying publication was launched at The Library Project in Dublin.

Garden of Eden Series by Ishmael Claxton | Shot with the LomoChrome Purple 35 mm ISO 100–400

Another highlight of the year was curating Black Noise at Gallery X. The exhibition brought together 22 Black artists from across Ireland and became far more than an exhibition. We expanded the programme to include a roundtable discussion exploring how the arts can build stronger communities, a live music jam session, poetry readings, contemporary dance performances, a collaborative zine-making workshop, and concluded with a healing circle. Seeing artists, audiences, and community groups come together across different disciplines made it one of the most meaningful projects I have worked on.

Looking ahead to the remainder of 2026, I will be co-curating the 7th annual ÍOVA Photography Collective Culture Night exhibition at REDS Gallery this September, continuing our commitment to showcasing emerging and established photographic practices from across Ireland.

I am also developing a new collaborative exhibition, Alternative Methods, which will open at Tøn Gallery in November. Created alongside four female artists, the project explores alternative approaches to curatorial practice by integrating pedagogy into the exhibition-making process. Rather than presenting a finished exhibition assembled by a single curator, we are collectively undertaking studio visits, conversations, and shared decision making, allowing the exhibition itself to emerge through collaboration and dialogue.

Dead Zoo in Blue, Ishmael Claxton is available now from The Library Project. To see more of Ishmael's work, visit his website.

Poco después del lanzamiento de la cámara analógica reutilizable de medio fotograma Simple Use, Lomography Tailandia le envió la cámara, precargada con película Lady Grey ISO 400, a Guy (dopamine.51) para que la pusiera a prueba. Echemos un vistazo a cómo Guy creó historias en medio fotograma y capturó el lado más tradicional de Bangkok entre luces y sombras.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White | Model: k_chayodom

¡Hola, Guy! ¿Podrías presentarte y contarnos cómo te iniciaste en la fotografía?

Hola a todos, me llamo Guy. Mi interés por la fotografía comenzó gracias a mi madre, a quien siempre le ha encantado tomar fotos. En casa teníamos cámaras analógicas, junto con una gran cantidad de álbumes llenos de imágenes de momentos importantes de nuestras vidas. Alrededor de 2018, me topé con una vieja cámara de carrete, así que decidí probar suerte. Me sentí atraído por los tonos suaves y cálidos, así como por la estética única de la fotografía analógica. Por esa misma época, la fotografía de película estaba experimentando un renacimiento aquí en Tailandia, lo que me inspiró a empezar a aprender sobre el medio de una forma más seria.

Actualmente trabajo como fotógrafo de retratos y realizo una gran variedad de proyectos, incluidos retratos conceptuales, fotos de graduación, cosplay y fotografía de ídolos. Presto mucha atención a la selección de atrezo (props), a combinar los colores de la ropa con las localizaciones y a elegir el tipo de película adecuado para cada sesión. Trabajo con película de color y de cine, además de emplear técnicas como el uso de flash e iluminación de colores para crear una atmósfera acorde con cada proyecto.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White

¿Dónde pusiste a prueba esta cámara? ¿Hubo algún tema o concepto detrás de la sesión?

Elegí fotografiar en la zona de Phra Nakhon, en Bangkok, concretamente en Charoen Krung, Yaowarat y Song Wat, ya que son lugares muy familiares para mí. Quería hacer las fotos al atardecer, justo cuando las tiendas empiezan a abrir y las calles se llenan de vendedores, turistas y una luz natural cambiante. Esto generaba unos contrastes preciosos entre las luces y las sombras.

En cuanto al concepto, buscaba que los dos fotogramas tuvieran una conexión, ya sea contando una misma historia o estableciendo un contraste entre ambas imágenes.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White

¿Cuál fue tu primera impresión de esta cámara? ¿Habías utilizado antes una cámara analógica de medio fotograma?

En primer lugar, me alegró mucho ver que se trata de una versión de medio fotograma de la cámara Simple Use y que además se puede recargar con nuevos carretes, algo que valoro muy positivamente. Es una cámara muy compacta y ligera, equipada con una lente gran angular y un flash integrado, lo que facilita muchísimo llevarla a todas partes. También me encanta el diseño de su cuerpo en tonos naranja y negro.

Anteriormente había usado una Olympus Pen EE. Es una cámara de medio fotograma muy divertida de usar, aunque su principal inconveniente es que carece de flash integrado, por lo que las fotos pueden quedar algo oscuras en condiciones de poca luz. Tras probar la Half-frame Simple Use, me pareció mucho más sencilla y práctica. El flash incorporado hace que no tenga que preocuparme tanto al fotografiar con luz escasa. Me da la tranquilidad de saber que puedo llevarla a cualquier sitio y aun así obtener buenos resultados.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White

¿Qué impresión te llevaste al ver los resultados revelados por el laboratorio?

La lente es más nítida de lo que esperaba, con un nivel de detalle y claridad fantásticos. La película ofrece un grano y unos contrastes muy agradables. En general, el resultado final superó mis expectativas tal y como lo había ideado. Me impresionó enormemente su rendimiento.

“Quería hacer las fotos al atardecer, justo cuando las tiendas empiezan a abrir y las calles se llenan de vendedores, turistas y una luz natural cambiante. Esto generaba unos contrastes preciosos entre las luces y las sombras”.

Al fotografiar en formato de medio fotograma, ¿sentiste que percibías las cosas de otra manera? ¿Cómo cambió tu aproximación a la fotografía en comparación con el formato completo?

Para mí resulta bastante familiar, ya que suelo disparar en orientación vertical de todos modos. La gran diferencia radica en pensar cómo emparejar los dos fotogramas y de qué manera pueden conectarse para relatar una historia. Eso hace que el proceso fotográfico sea mucho más divertido y me otorga mayor margen para incorporar ideas creativas.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White | Model: k_chayodom

¿Qué es lo que más te gusta de esta cámara y en qué se diferencia, bajo tu punto de vista, de las cámaras digitales u otras cámaras analógicas que hayas utilizado?

Me encanta lo fácil que es de usar. Es una cámara de medio fotograma que te permite realizar muchísimas tomas, y además puedes recargarla con diferentes películas, lo que ofrece una excelente relación calidad-precio. Su lente gran angular permite fotografiar en espacios reducidos. El flash integrado es otra de las funciones que más aprecio, ya que aporta diversión y dimensión a las imágenes. En comparación con cámaras profesionales más grandes, también noto que las personas frente al objetivo se muestran mucho más relajadas y menos cohibidas cuando disparo con ella.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White

Si tuvieras la oportunidad de volver a utilizar esta cámara, ¿dónde la llevarías o qué clase de momentos te gustaría capturar primero?

Me gustaría usarla en una boda, donde todo el mundo va arreglado y luce su mejor aspecto. Gracias a su diseño intuitivo, creo que sería ideal para inmortalizar momentos entrañables con la familia, los novios y el ambiente festivo entre los invitados. Pienso que si pasara la cámara de mano en mano para que todos tomaran fotos, obtendríamos una colección repleta de recuerdos inolvidables.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White | Model: k_chayodom

¿Hubo alguna fotografía en particular que te impresionara especialmente tomada con esta cámara? ¿Podrías contarnos la historia que hay detrás de ella?

La primera foto es la de un tuk-tuk en mitad de un cruce. Me quedé esperando allí un buen rato porque quería capturar el instante exacto en el que solo hubiera un vehículo en el centro de la intersección. Entonces, de forma inesperada, el conductor del tuk-tuk se saltó un semáforo en rojo ¡y así fue como conseguí esta toma! Jajaja.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White

La segunda foto es la de un joven modelo que, casualmente, es mi barbero habitual. A menudo hablábamos de fotografía cada vez que iba a cortarme el pelo, así que esta vez por fin le pedí que fuera mi modelo. Jajaja. Le hizo mucha ilusión; después de tanto tiempo oyéndome hablar de fotografía, dijo que ya era hora de probar suerte por sí mismo.

Shortly after the launch of the Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera, Lomography Thailand sent the camera, preloaded with Lady Grey ISO 400 film, to Guy (dopamine.51) to put it to the test. Let’s take a look at how Guy created half-frame stories and captured the old town side of Bangkok in light and shadow.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White | Model: k_chayodom

Hi, Guy! Could you please introduce yourself and tell us how you first got into photography?

Hi, everyone, my name is Guy. My interest in photography started with my mother, who has always loved taking photos. We had film cameras at home, along with lots of photo albums with photos of important moments in our lives. Around 2018, I came across an old film camera, so I decided to give it a try. I was drawn to the soft, warm tones and unique look of film photography. Around the same time, film photography was making a comeback here in Thailand, which inspired me to start learning more seriously about photography.

Currently, I work as a portrait photographer, shooting a variety of projects including conceptual portraits, graduation photos, cosplay, and idol photography. I pay close attention to selecting props, matching the colors of outfits with the locations, and choosing the right type of film for each shoot. I work with color film and motion picture film, as well as techniques such as flash and colored lighting, to create an atmosphere that suits each project.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White

Where did you take this camera for a spin? Was there any theme or concept behind the shoot?

I chose to shoot around the Phra Nakhon side of Bangkok, particularly in Charoen Krung, Yaowarat, and Song Wat, as these all are familiar places for me. I wanted to shoot in the evening, especially when the shops were starting to open and the streets were filled with vendors, tourists, and changing natural light. This created beautiful contrasts between light and shadow.

For the concept, I wanted the two frames to have a connection, whether by telling the same story or creating a contrast between the two images.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White

What was your first impression of this camera? Have you used a half-frame film camera before?

First of all, I was really happy to see that it’s a half-frame version of the Simple Use Camera and that it can be reloaded with new films, which is something I really like. The camera is very compact and lightweight, comes with a wide-angle lens and a built-in flash, making it very easy to carry around. I also really like the orange-and-black body.

I’ve used an Olympus Pen EE before. It’s a really fun half-frame camera to shoot with, although one downside is that it doesn’t have a built-in flash, so photos can turn out a little dark in low-light situations. After trying the Half-frame Simple Use, I found it much easier and more convenient to use. The built-in flash means I don’t have to worry as much when shooting in low light. It gives me peace of mind knowing that I can take it anywhere and still get good results.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White

What was your impression when you got the results back from the lab?

The lens is sharper than I expected, with great detail and clarity. The film has nice grain and contrasts. Overall, the results turned out just as I had envisioned. I was really impressed with how well it performed.

“I wanted to shoot in the evening, especially when the shops were starting to open and the streets were filled with vendors, tourists, and changing natural light. This created beautiful contrasts between light and shadow.”

When shooting in half-frame format, did you find yourself seeing things differently? How did your approach to photography change compared to shooting in full frame?

For me, it feels quite similar because I usually shoot in portrait orientation anyway. The main difference is thinking about how to pair the two frames and how they can connect to tell a story. It makes shooting more fun and gives me more room to incorporate creative ideas.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White | Model: k_chayodom

What do you like most about this camera, and how do you think it differs from digital or other film cameras you’ve used?

I love the fact that it's very easy to use. It's a half-frame camera that lets you take a lot of photos, and you can even reload it with different films, which makes it great value for money. The wide-angle lens allows you to shoot in narrow spaces. The built-in flash is another feature I really like, as it adds more fun and dimension to the images. Compared to larger professional cameras, I also find that people in front of the camera tend to feel more relaxed and less self-conscious when I’m shooting with it.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White

If you had the chance to use this camera again, where would you take it, or what kind of moments would you want to capture first?

I’d like to use it in a wedding, where everyone is dressed up and looking their best. With its user-friendly design, I think it would be great for capturing warm moments with family and the bride and groom, as well as the fun atmosphere among the guests. I believe that if I handed the camera around and let everyone take photos, we’d end up with a collection full of memorable moments.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White | Model: k_chayodom

Were there any particular photos you were especially impressed with from this camera? Could you tell us the story behind them?

The first photo is of a tuk-tuk in the middle of an intersection. I stood there waiting for quite a while because I wanted to capture the moment when there was only one vehicle in the middle of the intersection. Then, unexpectedly, the tuk-tuk driver ran a red light, and I ended up getting this shot! Hahaha.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White

The second photo is of a young male model who happens to be my regular barber. We often talked about photography whenever I went to get a haircut, so this time I finally asked him to be my model. Hahaha. He was really happy about it – after hearing me talk about photography so much, he said it was time for him to give it a try himself.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White | Model: k_chayodom

If you had the chance to take the Half-frame Simple Use out for another shoot, what song would you choose as the soundtrack?

I’d choose Perfect Timing by Ray Saetta. The beat and vocals fit perfectly with the atmosphere of walking around and taking photos, especially when shooting in black and white.

© dopamine.51 | Half-frame Simple Use Reloadable Film Camera Black & White

Do you have any advice or tips for anyone trying the Half-frame Simple Use for the first time?

I’d say it’s really easy to use. It has a built-in flash, is convenient to take with you when traveling, and offers great value for money. Plus, you can reload it with new rolls of film. I also think it makes a great gift for a friend or partner, or a fun camera to have at events where everyone can take turns using it.

Lastly, I’d love for everyone to follow my work on Instagram at dopamine.51. If you’d like to chat, ask for advice, or are interested in hiring me for film or digital photography, as well as camera and photography gear reviews, feel free to get in touch. I hope everyone enjoys taking photos. Thank you!

Resulta que la poesía y la fotografía comparten un lenguaje profundamente común. La creadora afincada en los Países Bajos Nikki, conocida también como Satellite June, demuestra exactamente eso en su nuevo libro, The Many Deaths of My Mother. Armada con una máquina de escribir y una colección de cámaras analógicas, se propuso enfrentar su dolor. Ya sea en blanco y negro o en color, en formato medio o de 35 mm, el lector puede contemplar imágenes de una hondura sumamente personal. En este artículo, nos habla abiertamente sobre los efectos catárticos de crear arte.

© @ satellitejune

¡Hola, Nikki! Es un verdadero placer conocerte. Me alegra mucho tener la oportunidad de entrevistarte a raíz de tu reciente libro, The Many Deaths of My Mother. Pero antes, ¿podrías presentarte brevemente a los lectores de la revista Lomography?

¡Hola! Soy Nikki, una fotógrafa analógica afincada en los Países Bajos que trabaja bajo el nombre artístico de Satellite June. Me encanta encontrar la magia en la vida cotidiana: esos momentos tranquilos y a menudo pasados por alto que te piden detenerte y volver a mirar. En mi obra tiendo puentes entre el arte y la salud mental, utilizando la fotografía como una forma de explorar la vulnerabilidad y unos paisajes interiores que no siempre son fáciles de expresar con palabras.

© @ satellitejune

Tu libro es un hermoso homenaje tanto a la poesía como a la fotografía. Cuéntanos, ¿cuándo empezó a tomar forma la idea de combinar ambos medios?

En realidad, todo ocurrió de manera muy natural; para mí, un día normal comienza escribiendo mis páginas matutinas y saliendo a dar un paseo. Durante esa caminata, siempre miro a mi alrededor para hallar la magia en la vida cotidiana: sombras que bailan, formas hermosas, colores que despiertan mi interés. Siempre llevo una pequeña cámara en el bolso a todas partes para poder capturar un instante que me haga sentir algo. Mi libro es la combinación de ambos hábitos.

© @ satellitejune

Mirando atrás, me di cuenta de que fotografiaba durante los periodos en los que no podía explicar mis sentimientos. Las imágenes me ayudaban a comprender por lo que estaba pasando. Cuando la vida volvía a ser un poco más ligera, las palabras surgían de manera natural. Escribir poesía se convirtió en otra forma de procesar esas vivencias. Unir la fotografía y la poesía en el libro resultó inevitable; se complementan mutuamente.

A lo largo del libro utilizas exclusivamente fotografías analógicas. ¿Por qué decidiste emplear película en lugar de, digamos, imágenes digitales?

Desde el momento en que empecé a hacer fotos, lo he hecho todo con una cámara analógica. Ni siquiera he intentado hacerlo en digital; me enamoré de la película de inmediato. Me encantaba la sensación de estar presente en el momento y así aprendí a confiar en mí misma y en mi visión. Soy una gran apasionada de la textura granulada y la sensación nostálgica que la película aporta a mis imágenes; encaja a la perfección con la atmósfera de ensueño que me gusta crear.

© @ satellitejune

Al hojear tu obra publicada, encontramos muchos autorretratos. ¿Por qué era importante para ti que acompañaran a tus poemas?

La fotografía se convirtió en una forma instintiva de procesar lo que no podía expresar con palabras. Los autorretratos nunca trataron de mostrarme a los demás, sino de reencontrarme a mí misma. En los periodos en los que sentía que simplemente estaba sobreviviendo, la cámara me ayudaba a preguntarme: «¿Cómo estoy, de verdad?». Esas fotografías se transformaron en un silencioso diario visual de mi mundo interior.

© @ satellitejune

En la introducción de tu libro escribiste que, tras terminarlo, «sientes que has aprendido a sostener la pérdida viva de otra manera». ¿Puedes contarnos más sobre cómo la realización de esta pieza creativa te ayudó a transitar y procesar el duelo?

La idea del libro cobró vida cuando estuve revisando mis fotografías de diez años y advertí un hilo conductor: fotografiaba para lidiar con sentimientos abrumadores, y en muchos de ellos ese sentimiento era el duelo. Cuando no encontraba las palabras, recurría a la fotografía. Mirando atrás ahora, puedo ver que el duelo ha sido una parte importante de mi vida, y creo que la mayoría de las personas también experimentan formas de duelo a lo largo de su existencia.

«Unir la fotografía y la poesía en el libro resultó inevitable; se complementan mutuamente.»

A veces es una gran ola de dolor, a veces es tan solo una pequeña salpicadura. El duelo es mucho más común de lo que pensamos; simplemente es algo de lo que no se habla mucho cuando no se trata del tipo de duelo "evidente" que surge cuando alguien muere. También hay duelo al terminar una relación, al echar de menos a una versión anterior de uno mismo, al añorar una etapa de la vida, al extrañar amistades que cambiaron a medida que fuiste creciendo, etcétera.

Así que supongo que, al hacer el libro, aprendí que tomar fotos es mi manera de lidiar con los sentimientos pesados. En mi fotografía plasmo tanto los momentos difíciles como las cosas hermosas y mundanas, y eso resulta sumamente reconfortante para mi mente.

© @ satellitejune

La pérdida y el duelo son profundamente personales. ¿Qué te impulsó a compartir estos sentimientos tan vulnerables con el mundo?

Me llevó mucho tiempo encontrar el valor para compartir este trabajo. Las fotografías se hicieron durante un periodo en el que intentaba sobrevivir más que crear. Nunca tuvieron la intención de ser un proyecto; eran una forma de aferrarurme a mí misma.

Con el tiempo, comprendí que el título, The Many Deaths of My Mother, podría pertenecer a cualquiera. Podrías sustituir la palabra "madre" por la salud, el amor, el hogar o el futuro que imaginaste. Los detalles de nuestras historias pueden diferir, pero los sentimientos que conllevan suelen ser sumamente similares.

Compartir esta obra es mi manera de abrir espacio para esos sentimientos. Espero que el libro ofrezca reconocimiento, consuelo y permiso para vivir un duelo por aquellas experiencias que rara vez se reconocen. Si mi vulnerabilidad permite que otra persona reconozca su propia vivencia, encuentre palabras para emociones que no ha podido nombrar o simplemente se sienta un poco menos sola, entonces compartirlo merece la pena. Creo que cuanto más nos permitimos hablar con honestidad sobre el duelo, menos aislado se vuelve.

© @ satellitejune

Dado que tenemos a muchos entusiastas de la fotografía leyendo nuestra revista, debemos preguntar: ¿con qué cámaras elegiste trabajar para este proyecto? ¿Hubo algún equipo de Lomography involucrado?

La mayor parte de mi obra está tomada con mi cámara principal: la Canon AE-1. Además de esa, utilicé una Mamiya C3, una Nikon F3, una Polaroid Spirit 600 CL, la Kodak Ektar H35 y la cámara Lomo’Instant Square Glass. Las fotografías del libro son una recopilación de mi trabajo de los últimos 10 años, así que utilicé una gran variedad de cámaras a lo largo del camino.

© @ satellitejune | Disparado con la Lomo’Instant Square Glass Camera

¿Y qué hay de las películas? ¡Estamos casi seguros de vislumbrar algo de Lomography Redscale por ahí!

¡Ja, ja, así es! Me encanta la película Redscale. Me fascina cómo aporta una sensación muy cálida pero a la vez de otro mundo, como si estuvieras adentrándote en un universo onírico. Aparte de esa, utilicé muchas emulsiones diferentes: Kodak Gold 200, Cinestill 800T, Kodak Portra 160/400/800, Fujifilm 400, Ilford HP5 y Polaroid.

Me encanta seguir experimentando y encontrar las películas que se ajustan al estado de ánimo que quiero fotografiar. Alternar entre tonos más fríos o más cálidos, o matices más verdosos o amarillentos, aporta mayor profundidad a mi obra. Me gusta pensar que «edito» mis fotografías incluso antes de pulsar el disparador. Elegir la cámara y el tipo de película ya forma parte del proceso creativo; determinan la atmósfera mucho antes de que la imagen exista.

© @ satellitejune

As it turns out, poetry and photography share a deeply common language. Netherlands-based creator Nikki, also known as Satellite June, proves exactly that in her new book, The Many Deaths of My Mother. Armed with a typewriter and a collection of film cameras, she set out to confront her grief. Whether in black and white or color, medium or 35 mm format, the reader gets to see images turned deeply personal. In this article, she opens up about the cathartic effects of making art.

© @ satellitejune

Hi, Nikki! It is so lovely to meet you. I'm really happy to have the chance to interview you on your recent book, The Many Deaths of My Mother. But first, could you briefly introduce yourself to the readers of Lomography Magazine?

Hi! I'm Nikki, a film photographer based in the Netherlands, working under the artist name Satellite June. I love finding magic in everyday life – the quiet, often overlooked moments that ask you to slow down and look again. In my work, I build bridges between art and mental health, using photography as a way to explore vulnerability and inner landscapes that are not always easy to put into words.

© @ satellitejune

Your book is a beautiful homage to both poetry and photography. Tell us, when did the idea of combining these two media start to take shape?

It all happened very naturally, actually; a regular day for me is starting the day writing my morning pages and going for a walk. During that walk, I always look around me to find magic in everyday life; shadows that are dancing, beautiful shapes, colors that spark my interest. I always have a little camera in my bag everywhere I go, so I can capture a moment that makes me feel something. My book is a combination of both these habits of mine.

© @ satellitejune

Looking back, I realized I photographed during the periods when I couldn't explain my feelings. The images helped me understand what I was going through. When life became a little lighter again, the words followed naturally. Writing poetry became another way of processing those experiences. Bringing photography and poetry together in the book felt inevitable – they complete one another.

Throughout the book, you use solely analogue photos. Why did you decide to use film instead of, say, digital images?

From the moment I started taking photographs, I've done everything with an analogue camera. I never even tried doing it digitally; I fell in love with film straight away. I loved the feeling of being in the moment and learned to trust myself and my vision a lot this way. I am a big fan of the grainy, nostalgic feel film gives my images; it matches the dreamy vibe I like to create.

© @ satellitejune

When browsing through your published work, we find many self-portraits. Why was it important for you to have them accompany your poems?

Photography became an instinctive way of processing what I couldn't put into words. The self-portraits were never about showing myself to other people; they were about finding myself again. During periods where I felt like I was simply surviving, the camera helped me to ask, “How am I, really?” Those photographs became a quiet visual diary of my inner world.

© @ satellitejune

In the introduction to your book, you wrote that after finishing it, you “feel that you have learned how to hold living loss differently”. Can you tell us more about how completing this creative piece helped you navigate and process grief?

The idea for the book came to life when I was browsing through my ten years' worth of photographs and noticed a common thread: I photographed to deal with overwhelming feelings, and in a lot of them, that was grief. When I couldn’t find the words, I turned to photography. Looking back now, I can see that grief has been a major part of my life, and I think most people experience forms of grief throughout their lives as well.

“Bringing photography and poetry together in the book felt inevitable – they complete one another.”

Sometimes it’s a big wave of grief, sometimes it’s a little splash. Grieving is way more common than we think; it’s just something that isn’t talked about a lot when it’s not the “obvious” kind of grief when somebody dies. There is also grief in ending a relationship, missing an old version of yourself, missing a time in your life, missing friendships that changed as you got older, etc.

So, I guess, from making the book, I learned that taking photographs is a way for me to deal with heavy feelings. In my photography, I capture both the hard times, as well as the beautiful, mundane things, and it works really soothing for my mind.

© @ satellitejune

Loss and grief are deeply personal. What made you share these vulnerable feelings with the world?

It took me a long time to find the courage to share this work. The photographs were made during a period when I was trying to survive rather than create. They were never intended as a project; they were a way of holding on to myself.

Over time, I realized that the title, The Many Deaths of My Mother , could belong to anyone. You could replace the word mother with health, love, home, or the future you imagined. The details of our stories may differ, but the feelings they carry are often remarkably similar.

Sharing this work is my way of creating space for those feelings. I hope the book offers recognition, comfort, and permission to grieve experiences that are rarely acknowledged. If my vulnerability allows someone else to recognize their own experience, to find language for feelings they haven't been able to name, or simply to feel a little less alone, then sharing it feels worthwhile. I believe that the more we allow ourselves to speak honestly about grief, the less isolated it becomes.

© @ satellitejune

Since we have a lot of photography geeks reading our magazine, we have to ask: what cameras did you choose to work with for this project? Was there any Lomography gear involved?

Most of my work is shot on my main camera – the Canon AE-1. In addition to that, I used a Mamiya C3, a Nikon F3, a Polaroid Spirit 600 CL, Kodak Ektar H35, and the Lomo’Instant Square Glass Camera. The photographs in the book are a compilation of my work from the past 10 years, so I used a lot of different cameras along the way.

© @ satellitejune | Shot on Lomo’Instant Square Glass Camera

How about the film stocks? We're pretty sure we spot some Lomography Redscale in there!

Hah, that’s right! I love the Redscale film stock. I love how it feels really warm, but also otherworldly, like you’re entering a dream world. Besides that, I used a lot of different films: Kodak Gold 200, Cinestill 800T, Kodak Portra 160/400/800, Fujifilm 400, Ilford HP5, and Polaroid.

I love to keep on experimenting and finding the films that fit the mood I want to photograph. Switching between cooler/warmer tones, or more greenish or yellowish tones, adds more depth to my work. I like to think that I “edit” my photographs before I even press the shutter. Choosing the camera and film stock is already part of the creative process; they determine the atmosphere long before the image exists.

© @ satellitejune | Shot on Lomography Redscale 35mm

Poetry is obviously a massive part of the book as well. Can you tell us a bit about your writing process? Is it purely spontaneous, or perhaps more structured and organized?

A while ago, I got a typewriter as a gift from a friend, and I love the feeling of writing on it. The sound is lovely as well, and it fits my analogue approach in my work. It helps you to be in the moment more, to just focus on writing. During the book-making process, something magical happened: on some days, I could just feel that there was a poem that needed to be written. I would sit down and start writing, and it would just flow easily. I couldn’t stop thinking about the book Big Magic by Elizabeth Gilbert when that happened.

© @ satellitejune

Last, but not least – can we expect any similar projects from you in the future?

I'm interested in expanding beyond photography and exploring how grief, care, and connection can be experienced through different materials and rituals. I'm not entirely sure where that research will lead me yet, but that's exactly what excites me.

Stay updated on Satellite June’s projects by following her Instagram Page and definitely check out her new book here!

Hemos invitado a @filmlife_ww a utilizar la cámara analógica Lomo MC-A como herramienta creativa. Combinada con los carretes Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 y Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800, amplía su objetivo desde la fotografía de calle cotidiana hasta la preservación de la cultura local de Hong Kong.

Al documentar recuerdos colectivos en vías de extinción, como los letreros de neón, explora el delicado equilibrio entre «la imagen y los límites» en la fotografía urbana. A través de sus visuales, intenta congelar la calidez persistente de la ciudad, invitando a los lectores a reparar y registrar esas escenas aparentemente ordinarias que poseen un profundo peso cultural.

© @filmlife_ww | Cámara analógica Lomo MC-A con Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 y Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

¡Hola, @filmlife_ww! ¡Bienvenido de nuevo a la Revista Lomography! ¿Qué has estado haciendo últimamente?

¡Hola a todos, es genial volver a conectar con ustedes! Me gustaría agradecer a Lomography por prestarme la cámara analógica Lomo MC-A y compartir este trabajo con sus lectores. Últimamente, me he esforzado mucho por encontrar un equilibrio entre el trabajo y la vida personal. Durante los últimos seis meses, me he alejado de las tomas callejeras espontáneas y cinematográficas para centrarme más en proyectos de estilo documental. También he asistido a más exposiciones de fotografía y eventos comunitarios en busca de inspiración fresca.

© @filmlife_ww | Cámara analógica Lomo MC-A con Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 y Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

Por favor, compártanos algunos momentos de tu tiempo con la cámara. ¿A dónde fuiste y qué capturaste?

Para este proyecto, decidí desplazar mi perspectiva fotográfica de los barrios locales a la preservación cultural. La serie también incluye una gran cantidad de instantáneas que capturan las diversas facetas de la vida urbana cotidiana y los ritmos de la comunidad. Letreros de neón, dai pai dongs (puestos de comida al aire libre), salas de mahjong, clubes nocturnos, andamios de bambú y puestos de mercado tradicionales encontraron un lugar frente a mi objetivo.

Estos elementos son escenas que los hongkoneses dan por sentadas: cosas por las que pasamos en la calle y que se funden silenciosamente en cada rincón de la ciudad. Debido a que son tan familiares, es posible que la gente no les preste mucha atención. Sin embargo, estas vistas, objetos, ladrillos y azulejos aparentemente ordinarios portan el patrimonio cultural y el contexto histórico de Hong Kong.

Merece la pena mencionar en particular las historias que hay detrás de los letreros de neón. Las sombras persistentes de los clubes nocturnos en Portland Street, en Mong Kok, son testigos de la bulliciosa y glamurosa vida nocturna de Hong Kong en las décadas de 1980 y 1990, y registran cómo solían converger las multitudes bajo el resplandor de los neones. Trasladándonos a Central, «Ser Wong Fun» ha preservado su oficio tradicional centenario desde su fundación en 1895. Empezando con un solo plato de sopa de serpiente, no solo ha mantenido vivos los sabores clásicos cantoneses, sino que también se ha convertido en un hito inolvidable en Soho.

Por otro lado, el histórico establecimiento «Tak Hing Dried Seafood» en Yau Ma Tei protege la calidez de los hongkoneses de una manera diferente, construyendo confianza a través de sopas meticulosamente preparadas y una reputación perdurable, sirviendo silenciosamente al vecindario durante más de medio siglo con una dedicación discreta pero firme. Cada historia, moldeada por el tiempo, reconstruye silenciosamente la silueta de esta ciudad.

© @filmlife_ww | Cámara analógica Lomo MC-A con Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 y Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

¿Cuál fue tu primera impresión de la Lomo MC-A?

En el momento en que la sostuve, su apariencia me cautivó de inmediato. La carcasa de metal se sentía de gran calidad y, al combinarla con el cuero negro, el cuerpo lucía texturizado y a la vez elegante, con un diseño sumamente reconocible. El detalle más llamativo es, sin duda, el manifiesto de Lomography grabado en el cuerpo de la cámara: Todos aquellos que se sitúan ante un objetivo son iguales. Esto dota a la Lomo MC-A de una personalidad muy marcada.

Lomography siempre ha sido un símbolo de rebelión e individualismo en el mundo del celuloide, y esta cámara lo exhibe por completo.

«A medida que continúa el desmantelamiento, tal vez algún día tengamos que entrar en un museo solo para ver el brillo del neón».

¿Cómo se comportó durante las tomas casuales y cotidianas?

Para ser honesto, como alguien acostumbrado a las cámaras réflex manuales tradicionales, me tomó un momento adaptarme a la Lomo MC-A porque es increíblemente ligera. Sin embargo, tanto los principiantes como los usuarios experimentados pueden tomarla y usarla con total facilidad. A pesar de ser compacta y portátil, la MC-A cuenta con una pantalla LCD que muestra el contador de fotogramas y el modo de enfoque, lo que me permite consultar la información de disparo de un solo vistazo.

Antes de la sesión, tenía muchas ganas de comprobar su calidad de imagen y en qué se diferenciaba de las cámaras de película tradicionales. Para esta serie, utilicé dos películas de alto contraste: Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800 y Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400. El rendimiento nocturno fue especialmente sorprendente.

Tanto los tonos de color como la profundidad de campo ofrecieron una textura muy cercana a la de una cámara de película tradicional. Como cámara de focal fija de 32 mm, su desempeño con gran angular también es excelente. El único pequeño inconveniente es que la cámara se apaga sola de vez en cuando durante el uso; sería aún mejor si este punto pudiera mejorarse ligeramente.

© @filmlife_ww | Cámara analógica Lomo MC-A con Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 y Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

¿Tienes algún consejo para otros entusiastas de la fotografía que deseen acercarse más a sus sujetos en la fotografía de calle?

He reflexionado sobre esta pregunta en repetidas ocasiones. Encontrar el equilibrio entre lograr una buena foto y respetar los límites es un reto al que todo fotógrafo callejero debe enfrentarse. Según mi experiencia, cuando fotografío escenas de interior, como la dinámica de la gente dentro de un cha chaan teng (café de estilo hongkonés), suelo consumir primero en el local y tomo las fotos bajo ese contexto para no interrumpir su negocio.

Una de las claves de la fotografía de calle es la velocidad. Una gran obra suele nacer en un abrir y cerrar de ojos. Por lo tanto, antes de presionar el disparador, observa primero, compón la toma en tu mente y luego dispara con decisión cuando el momento sea el adecuado, minimizando así cualquier interferencia con el sujeto. Para los principiantes, se puede empezar con una lente de focal más larga para disparar desde una «distancia social» cómoda. A medida que adquieras experiencia, podrás cambiar gradualmente a una lente focal fija de gran angular, aprendiendo a observar las sutiles interacciones entre las personas y su entorno, fundiéndote con la escena y juzgando el instante preciso para capturarla.

https://www.lomography.com/magazine/3588.content_original:
We have invited @filmlife_ww to use the Lomo MC-A Film Camera as a creative tool. Paired with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 and Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800, he expands his lens from everyday street photography to the preservation of local Hong Kong culture.

By documenting vanishing collective memories like neon signs, he explores the delicate balance between “imagery and boundaries” in street photography. Through his visuals, he attempts to freeze the city's lingering warmth, inviting readers to notice and record the seemingly ordinary scenes that carry profound cultural weight.

© @filmlife_ww | Lomo MC-A Film Camera with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 and Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

Hello @filmlife_ww! Welcome back to Lomography Magazine! What have you been up to lately?

Hello everyone, it’s great to connect with you all again! I’d like to thank Lomography for lending me the Lomo MC-A film camera, and share this body of work with your readers. Lately, I’ve been trying hard to strike a balance between work and life. Over the past six months, I’ve stepped back from spontaneous, cinematic street shoots to focus more on documentary-style projects. I’ve also been attending more photography exhibitions and community events to seek fresh inspiration.

© @filmlife_ww | Lomo MC-A Film Camera with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 and Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

Please share some moments from your time with the camera. Where did you go, and what did you capture?

For this project, I decided to shift my photographic perspective from local neighborhoods to cultural preservation. The series also includes plenty of snapshots capturing the diverse facets of daily city life and community rhythms. Neon signs, dai pai dongs (open-air food stalls), mahjong parlors, nightclubs, bamboo scaffolding, and old-school market stalls all found a place before my lens.

These elements are scenes that Hong Kongers take for granted – things we pass by on the street that quietly blend into every corner of the city. Because they are so familiar, people might not pay close attention to them. However, these seemingly ordinary sights, objects, bricks, and tiles carry Hong Kong’s cultural heritage and historical context.

The stories behind the neon signs are particularly worth mentioning. The lingering shadows of the nightclubs on Portland Street in Mong Kok bear witness to Hong Kong's bustling, glamorous nightlife of the 1980s and 90s, recording how crowds used to converge under the neon glow. Moving over to Central, “Ser Wong Fun” has preserved its century-old traditional craft since its founding in 1895. Starting out with a single bowl of snake soup, it has not only kept classic Cantonese flavors alive but has also become an unforgettable landmark in Soho.

Meanwhile, the historic “Tak Hing Dried Seafood” in Yau Ma Tei protects the warmth of Hong Kongers in a different way, building trust through meticulously prepared soups and an enduring reputation, quietly serving the neighborhood for over half a century with low-key yet steadfast dedication. Each story, shaped by time, silently pieces together the silhouette of this city.

© @filmlife_ww | Lomo MC-A Film Camera with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 and Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

What was your first impression of the Lomo MC-A?

The moment I held it, I was immediately drawn to its appearance. The metal casing felt high-quality, and when paired with the black leather, the body looked textured yet stylish – a highly recognizable design. The most striking detail is undoubtedly the Lomography manifesto engraved on the camera body: All those who stand before a lens are equal. This adds a distinct personality to the Lomo MC-A.

Lomography has always been a symbol of rebellion and individualism in the film world, and this camera puts that entirely on display.

“As the dismantling continues, perhaps one day we will have to walk into a museum just to see the glow of neon.”

How did it perform during casual, everyday shooting?

To be honest, as someone accustomed to traditional manual SLRs, it took me a moment to adapt to the Lomo MC-A because it is incredibly lightweight. However, both beginners and experienced users can pick it up with ease. While being compact and portable, the MC-A features an LCD screen that displays the frame count and focus mode, allowing me to keep track of shooting info at a glance.

Before the shoot, I was really looking forward to seeing its image quality and how it differed from traditional film cameras. For this series, I used two high-contrast films: Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800 and Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400. The night performance was particularly surprising.

Both the color tones and depth of field delivered a texture very close to that of a traditional film camera. As a 32 mm fixed focal length camera, its wide-angle performance is also excellent. The only minor drawback is that the camera occasionally turns off automatically during shooting; it would be even better if this point could be slightly improved.

© @filmlife_ww | Lomo MC-A Film Camera with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 and Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

Do you have any advice for fellow photography enthusiasts who want to get closer to their subjects in street photography?

I have thought about this question repeatedly. Finding a balance between taking a good photo and respecting boundaries is a challenge every street photographer must face. In my experience, when shooting indoor scenes, like the dynamics of people inside a cha chaan teng (Hong Kong-style café), I usually patronize the shop first and take photos on the premise so as not to disrupt their business.

One of the keys to street photography is speed. A great piece of work is often born in the blink of an eye. Therefore, before pressing the shutter, observe first, compose the shot in your mind, and then shoot decisively when the timing is right, thereby minimizing interference with the subject. For beginners, you can start with a longer focal length lens to shoot from a comfortable “social distance”. As you gain experience, you can gradually switch to a wide-angle prime lens, learning to observe the subtle interactions between people and their environment, blending into the scene, and judging the right moment to capture it.

© @filmlife_ww | Lomo MC-A Film Camera with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 and Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

The Lomo MC-A offers features like autofocus, manual zone focusing, manual ISO, and exposure compensation. Did you control these settings yourself during the shoot, or did you let the camera decide?

The camera's wide array of adjustable features is undoubtedly one of its greatest strengths. When doing street photography, having higher manual control offers greater flexibility, so I preferred using manual settings for most of the shoot. Because street photography is easily affected by changing environments and lighting, manually adjusting the aperture, ISO, and focus allows me to flexibly set the most appropriate parameters based on the subject.

That said, I also tried the autofocus function during the shoot; for instance, in the shot taken at Pak Bo Tong in Sham Shui Po, the subject came out very sharp, and the result was quite good. Additionally, the camera is equipped with a multiple exposure function. This versatile design gave me even more creative options when it came to composition.

© @filmlife_ww | Lomo MC-A Film Camera with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 and Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

Which photograph from this series is your favorite, and why?

That’s a tough one! There are quite a few pieces from this series that I really love. But if I had to choose the one that left the deepest impression, it would have to be this one. The photo was taken at dusk, capturing the flow of the crowd heading home after work just as the city’s daily hustle was winding down. In the frame, the long, stretching staircase and handrail pull the viewer's eye toward an unseen horizon, making the entire movement feel like an extension of a singular rhythm.

Converging to the exact same beat within that narrow, confined space, the crowd weaves together Hong Kong's fast-paced yet orderly stride, beautifully showcasing the inherent tension and energy of the city's pulse.

© @filmlife_ww | Lomo MC-A Film Camera with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

If you had to choose a song to represent the feeling of shooting with the Lomo MC-A, what would it be?

I would choose Eason Chan's Salon. The Lomo MC-A gives me a highly creative shooting experience, it feels grounded yet rebellious, projecting an unconstrained attitude. It embodies the spirit of living in the moment and embracing reality, reminding us to experience life with heightened sensitivity and to use our cameras to record unpolished fragments of existence.

Just as “Salon” uses photography as a metaphor for life, the key lies in capturing the sheer density of living. When we learn to cherish the present and freeze each moment in time, life becomes real, rather than vanishing into thin air like smoke.

© @filmlife_ww | Lomo MC-A Film Camera with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 and Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

Lastly, is there anything else you’d like to share with us? Any upcoming projects or parting words for our readers?

First, let me share a fun piece of trivia about neon signs. The rise of neon lights in Hong Kong began after World War II. With the rapid development of post-war industry, businesses of all kinds – restaurants, nightclubs, pawn shops – used neon signs as advertising tools, reaching a golden era in the 1980s and 90s. Some local neon signs even set Guinness World Records. In 1973, the National neon sign on the exterior wall of the Majestic Theatre in Jordan was made using over 4,000 neon tubes, becoming the largest in the world at the time. In 1982, the Citizen Watches neon sign in Causeway Bay broke the record with tubes stretching a total of three miles. By 1990, the Panasonic neon sign broke the record yet again, becoming the longest neon sign globally at the time before it was officially retired in 2021.

Today, the number of neon signs in Hong Kong has plummeted to around 224, with about 139 in Kowloon and 85 on Hong Kong Island. Over the past five years, more than 16,000 signs (including neon ones) have been removed, turning what was once a brilliant city icon into a vanishing cultural heritage. It feels as though some landscapes are destined to become specimens of a bygone era.

Online commentators often note that Hong Kong is no longer what it used to be, losing its uniqueness to homogenization. While conceptualizing this project, I couldn't help but wonder: under the crushing gears of time, what can truly remain unchanged for half a century? Some places have witnessed such beauty that people form deep attachments to them, making it difficult to let go even when they become unrecognizable. Since we cannot reverse the tides of time, we can use images as a form of preservation, reclaiming those familiar scenes through the lens. This body of work is precisely about holding onto the city's remaining warmth and defining a Hong Kong that belongs to me.

© @filmlife_ww | Lomo MC-A Film Camera with the Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 400 and Lomography Color Negative 35 mm ISO 800

“Act as a phonograph – that is the finest creed for any creative youth.” I would also like to invite our readers to become active participants in cultural preservation. Pay a little more attention during your daily commutes, and document the city's unique symbols in your own way. What truly deserves to be protected is often not just the imminent demolition making the news, but those seemingly ordinary everyday scenes that carry the weight of time.

Only when they are seen and cared for do they stand a chance of living on. As the dismantling continues, perhaps one day we will have to walk into a museum just to see the glow of neon. But the moments frozen by the shutter and the weight carried by light and shadow will endure in these images, never to disappear.

We would like to thank @filmlife_ww for participating in this shoot and sharing his heartfelt insights.
